news.content_original: The remains of a northern gannet, probably a victim of avian influenza, washed up on a beach – H5N1 is now a conservation threat to at least 40 bird species, according to BirdLife International. Photograph: Matthijs Wetterauw/Alamy The remains of a northern gannet, probably a victim of avian influenza, washed up on a beach – H5N1 is now a conservation threat to at least 40 bird species, according to BirdLife International. Photograph: Matthijs Wetterauw/Alamy Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow? As the IUCN global conservation body prepares to update its red list of endangered species, scientists explain why calculating the true toll of a pandemic is so hard I t began with the brown skuas. The migratory seabirds had arrived on the sub-Antarctic island of South Georgia in 2023, harbouring a deadly passenger. Within months, the southern elephant seals that had come ashore to breed became sick. Mothers and newborn pups were weak and trembling, with many struggling to breathe. What followed was a horrific mass casualty event, caused by the highly infectious avian influenza (H5N1). By 2025, more than 53,000 female elephant seals had died on South Georgia. That is especially alarming, scientists say, because the island is home to more than half of the global breeding population . A highly potent strain of the bird flu virus, which first began circulating in the northern hemisphere in 2021, has now spread to four of the five main southern elephant seal populations. In some South Atlantic colonies, more than 90% of newborn pups have died , alongside about half of all adult females. A southern elephant seal with a pup at Gold harbour, South Georgia. By 2025, more than 53,000 female elephant seals had died on the island. Photograph: Ashley Cooper/Alamy “This is a horror show for wildlife,” says Ruth Cromie, coordinator of a UN taskforce on avian influenza and wildlife. “The scale of mortality is absolutely unprecedented.” In April, the mass deaths prompted the IUCN red list, the global authority responsible for assessing the extinction risks of wildlife, to downgrade the southern elephant seal’s conservation status by two categories, from “least concern” to “vulnerable”. It was the first time a species has had its extinction risk raised explicitly because of H5N1. Dead elephant seals on South Georgia in January 2026. Photograph: Jane Younger The IUCN listing notes that scientists suspect the global southern elephant seal population has declined by nearly a third, and models suggest many populations will take decades to recover. So far, scientists have found few antibodies to the disease among surviving animals. The southern elephant seal is just one species that has suffered catastrophic die-offs since H5N1 began burning its way through the world’s wildlife, killing hundreds of thousands of animals , if not millions. Avian influenza is now a threat to at least 40 bird species, according to BirdLife International , a global conservation partnership. And yet, no other animal – seal or bird – has seen its conservation status changed. But scientists warn that does not mean there are not more species being pushed to the brink by this deadly pathogen. A ssessing a species’ conservation threats is a painstaking scientific and bureaucratic process. To date, the red list has analysed nearly 176,000 species’ extinction risks, and aims to reach 260,000 species by 2030, as well as 142,000 reassessments. Most species are only reassessed by a panel of expert scientists once every decade or so – no matter the emerging threats they may face. The red list itself is updated two to three times a year. Birds are the exception. BirdLife International serves as the authority for assessing the world’s 11,000-plus bird species, reviewing hundreds of birds every year. For that reason, our understanding of the extinction risks of birds is better than for any other animal group. In an epidemic where birds are the foremost victim, that is obviously convenient. But there can still be a lag when deaths are coming faster than scientists can convene and publish under peer review. “We still need to get these things out there,” says Rob Martin, senior red list officer at BirdLife International. Northern gannets rest next to dead gannets on Rouzic Island, off the Brittany coast, in 2022. Photograph: F Tanneau/AFP/Getty Species are generally “uplisted” when they have experienced a sustained population decline over three generations, a small population is in decline or living within a restricted range, or calculations show that the species could become extinct in the near future, given existing population dynamics. Scientific uncertainty often underlies such reviews. Assessors need to know the animal’s baseline population before they can determine if it has crossed a threshold towards extinction. For many species, such figures are in short supply. And without knowing a species’ starting point, it is difficult to calculate the true toll of an outbreak. Scientists with BirdLife International say they are now focused on reassessing four species that have suffered H5N1 outbreaks large enough to affect their conservation outlook: the great skua, northern gannet, Peruvian pelican and Humboldt penguin. Great skuas courting on the Shetland Islands, off Scotland. Photograph: BSIP/Universal/Getty In Scotland, home to more than half of the world’s great skuas , the population of monitored colonies fell by 76% between 2021 and 2023. Meanwhile, the northern gannet, the largest seabird native to the North Atlantic, declined dramatically in two breeding populations in the UK as bird flu spread: by 43% at Bass Rock in Scotland between 2021 and 2024 and 47% at Grassholm in Wales between 2015 and 2024. These are two of the largest northern gannet colonies, and extrapolating from such figures would imply a steep population fall, say BirdLife International assessors, potentially qualifying the species for uplisting from “least concern”. But when scientists took a broader look , they found that the entire north-eastern Atlantic population had declined no more than 17% between 2013 and 2024. “Rushing to judgment a few years ago, with only partial data available and no sense of whether the whole population was declining, would have been premature and could have led to a misclassification,” BirdLife International scientists say. Martin cautions that it is important to prevent “kneejerk” uplisting after a mass mortality event, as listings such as “critically endangered” can trigger dozens of conservation funding proposals and divert government spending. “We need it to be a tool that the community can reliably use and say ‘we trust this,’” he says. Municipal workers collect dead pelicans in Lima, Peru, in November 2022 as another struggles to move. At least 13,000 birds had died by then along Peru’s Pacific coast. Photograph: G Pardo/AP About a fifth of the pelican population living in Peru’s marine protected areas are thought to have succumbed to bird flu in 2022 and 2023. But the Peruvian pelican is considered an abundant bird. “It’s difficult to get accurate numbers for the population pre- and post- [the H5N1 outbreak] because they’re in quite isolated areas without sufficient funding for monitoring,” says Martin. Counting the dead often poses an even greater hurdle, especially for migratory species that travel vast distances over oceans. “You usually don’t find most of the dead birds. If they die at sea, they’re lost,” says Wouter Langhout, a policy consultant at BirdLife International. The flightless Humboldt penguin, which spends most of its life on land, has made such tallies easier. In 2023, scientists counted nearly 3,000 dead penguins along Chile’s coasts, prompting another review of the already vulnerable species, which was last assessed in 2020. E ven when population and mortality numbers are easy to come by, spectacular mass die-offs – as gruesome as they may be – do not guarantee a species is inching towards extinction. For long-lived seabirds, large waterbirds and elephant seals that are slow to reproduce and late to sexually mature, a large loss of breeding adults can translate into severe population declines in just three generations – a key red-list criterion for uplisting. But fast-reproducing animals or those with abundant populations may be spared such long-term consequences, especially if more adult males die than fertile females. Antarctic fur seals in heavy snow on South Georgia as king penguins pass by. Photograph: Ben Cranke/naturepl.com In the case of the Antarctic fur seal, for example, far more males have succumbed to the disease than breeding females, says Jaume Forcada, a marine mammal expert and population biologist at the British Antarctic Survey who has studied Antarctic fur seals for 25 years. That is because male and female fur seals behave very differently. Whereas the males come ashore for about two months, often battling with one another on beaches, “when females arrive, they pup, and then they go out very quickly. They’re less exposed to other animals apart from the moment when they are rearing their pup,” Forcada says. In turn, “the males were very severely affected, whereas the females were absolutely fine. It’s like it was a completely different species. It hadn’t affected them.” If scientists uncover a population decline that would warrant uplisting, attributing it to avian influenza may not be cut and dried, Martin cautions. For example, BirdLife recently reassessed the African penguin, which was heavily affected by avian influenza. Although it was uplisted to critically endangered in 2024, assessors determined that food loss linked to commercial fisheries and the climate crisis – not bird flu – ultimately drove its decline. The carcass of an endangered Humboldt penguin on a beach in Vina del Mar, Chile, in 2023. Photograph: R Garrido/Reuters The 3,000 dead Humboldt penguins in Chile have also triggered debate among scientists. Penguins often drown in gill nets and 2023 was also an El Niño year, which may have had a hand in the birds’ deaths. “That year could be described as a ‘perfect storm’, which produced highly unfavourable conditions for Humboldt penguins,” says Alejandro Simeone, a scientist in the IUCN’s penguin specialist group. “While it is quite possible that some Humboldt penguins died from [avian influenza], current evidence makes it difficult to assess the true extent of the virus’s role in this decline,” Simeone says. I n the end, it may not be the most visible victims that are in the greatest peril. Birds with tiny isolated populations – often those inhabiting small islands – can quickly move towards extinction even if only a handful of individuals die. “For species that are already under threat and declining for other reasons, and then you put in something like avian influenza, that might be the thing that then pushes them over the edge ,” Cromie says. To date, scientists say they are not yet aware of any such cases from bird flu, but are anxiously monitoring Australia , where H5N1 was first detected on the mainland in June. The endangered regent honeyeater in an aviary at Sydney’s Taronga zoo this year, where vulnerable species of birds are being vaccinated against bird flu. Photograph: B de Marchi/AAP “A lot of Australian species still do have quite wide ranges, but there’s a very specific habitat that they rely on,” Martin says. The country is also home to a number of critically endangered birds that can be found nowhere else in the world, such as the orange-bellied parrot and the regent honeyeater. Waiting for uplisting, Cromie adds, may miss the bigger picture. “We have to be focusing on taking these other pressures off,” she says. “If we become very fixated on only waiting to do something because of a change of status, there’s such a lag there. We’ve got to be doing other things at the same time.” Already, fur seals and dolphins in Australian waters have begun to die from bird flu. And things are about to get worse for the now-vulnerable southern elephant seal. In August, the government’s Australian Antarctic Division said it would evacuate its research station on Macquarie Island in anticipation of mass seal die-offs if H5N1 reaches its shores. Macquarie is the last stronghold of southern elephant seals that, until recently, had remained untouched by the virus. Though the risk to human health is low, the agency said it hoped to prevent psychological distress for staff who could witness the deaths of thousands of newborn seal pups. About 5,000 of the world’s largest little penguin colony, on Australia’s Phillip Island, were vaccinated against H5N1. Photograph: Getty The next update to the list is due on 26 November, and proposals for new uplistings will next be discussed in January and February 2027. “Our biggest fear is always that we completely miss something that suddenly is critically endangered. That’s what we’re guarding against,” Martin says. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 13, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Rare H9N2 Influenza Mutation Reduces Viral Replication but Worsens Lung Damage by November 7, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Rare H9N2 Influenza Mutation Reduces Viral Replication but Worsens Lung Damage Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers characterized the phenotypic consequences of an amino acid loss at residue 227 within the hemagglutinin receptor-binding domain using isogenic reverse genetics viruses. While deletions within this specific domain represent a notable and rare evolutionary trajectory among genetically diverse H9N2 field strains, the finding demonstrates that viral burden alone does not reliably predict the severity of avian influenza disease. The targeted deletion, designated HAΔ227, is a naturally occurring mutation situated directly inside the hemagglutinin 220-loop, a structural segment that overlaps an essential antigenic epitope. In laboratory evaluations, introducing this deletion imposed a measurable fitness cost on the pathogen. Reverse genetics experiments revealed that the mutant virus exhibited altered functional coordination between viral surface glycoproteins, featuring enhanced hemagglutinin receptor-binding avidity alongside reduced apparent virion-associated neuraminidase activity. This compromised replicative capacity persisted during experimental animal trials, where chickens infected with the mutant strain exhibited reduced respiratory shedding in vivo compared to control strains. Paradoxically, despite lower viral replication and reduced shedding, birds infected with the HAΔ227 virus experienced more extensive pathological damage. Post-infection assessments documented more severe pulmonary lesions in the affected lung tissues. These pathological changes were accompanied by a pronounced dissociation between viral RNA load and clinical disease manifestations, confirming that lower pathogen burdens can coincide with heightened structural tissue injury during avian influenza infections. The disproportionate lung injury observed in infected chickens was linked to a sharply altered host immune response elicited by the mutant pathogen. Tissue and molecular analyses revealed significantly elevated levels of critical inflammatory signaling proteins following infection, specifically interferon-gamma, interleukin-10, interleukin-1beta, and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1. Biochemical characterization further demonstrated that the single-residue deletion at position 227 raised the pH threshold required for hemagglutinin-mediated membrane fusion and substantially altered antigenic relationships. The authors concluded that residue 227 represents a functionally vital site where a single deletion governs an evolutionary trade-off between replication efficiency and virulence. Although HAΔ227 viruses replicate less effectively in vitro and shed less abundantly in vivo, their capacity to induce intensified inflammatory responses and severe tissue damage demonstrates that monitoring viral loads alone may obscure the pathogenic potential of emerging avian influenza variants. news.title_original: Rare H9N2 Influenza Mutation Reduces Viral Replication but Worsens Lung Damage

analysis.time: The study was published on November 7, 2026, and the research findings were based on experiments conducted with the HAΔ227 mutation, which was identified as a rare mutation in H9N2 influenza viruses.
analysis.location_and_population: The research was conducted in a laboratory setting using chickens as experimental animals, focusing on the effects of the HAΔ227 mutation on avian influenza.
analysis.event: A rare H9N2 influenza mutation, HAΔ227, was characterized for its effects on viral replication and disease severity. The mutation was found to reduce viral replication but increase lung damage in infected chickens.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The HAΔ227 mutation was observed to reduce viral replication and shedding in vivo, but it caused more severe pulmonary lesions and elevated inflammatory responses in infected birds. These findings highlight the potential for monitoring viral loads alone to miss the pathogenic potential of emerging avian influenza variants.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study used reverse genetics and experimental animal trials to evaluate the mutation's effects. The results indicate a measurable fitness cost and altered immune responses, but no public health response or containment measures were reported.

analysis.brief_en: A study published on November 7, 2026, identified a rare H9N2 influenza mutation, HAΔ227, which reduces viral replication but increases lung damage in infected chickens. Researchers found that this mutation, located within the hemagglutinin 220-loop, imposes a measurable fitness cost on the virus, resulting in lower in vivo shedding and reduced respiratory replication. Despite these limitations, the mutation was linked to more severe pulmonary lesions and heightened inflammatory responses, including elevated levels of interferon-gamma, interleukin-10, interleukin-1beta, and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1. The findings suggest that monitoring viral loads alone may not capture the full pathogenic potential of emerging avian influenza variants. The study, conducted in a laboratory setting using reverse genetics and animal trials, highlights the complex relationship between viral replication efficiency and disease severity in avian influenza.

The study, conducted in a laboratory setting using reverse genetics and animal trials, highlights the complex relationship between viral replication efficiency and disease severity in avian influenza.

news.title_zh: 罕见的 H9N2 流感 突变 减少病毒复制但加剧肺损伤

news.content_zh: 2026 年 11 月 7 日发表的一项研究发现了一种罕见的 H9N2 流感 突变(HAΔ227),它会减少病毒复制,但会增加受感染鸡的肺部损伤。研究人员发现,位于血凝素 220 环内的 突变 对病毒造成了可测量的适应性成本,导致体内病毒脱落减少并减少了呼吸道复制。尽管存在这些限制,突变 仍与更严重的肺部病变和加剧的炎症反应有关,包括干扰素 γ、白细胞介素 10、白细胞介素 1β 和单核细胞趋化蛋白 1 水平升高。研究结果表明,仅监测病毒载量可能无法捕获新出现的 禽流感 变种的全部致病潜力。这项研究是在实验室环境中利用反向遗传学和动物试验进行的,强调了 禽流感 病毒复制效率与疾病严重程度之间的复杂关系。

Advertisement Avian influenza has been confirmed in an Oregon dairy herd for the first time, federal officials said Tuesday, making Oregon the 22nd state with infected cattle weeks after an outbreak in neighboring Washington was linked to 3 human infections, including 1 death.1,2 The herd was identified through Oregon’s ongoing surveillance for the virus in dairy cattle and had consistently tested negative before the detection, the US Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) said in a news release. The agency did not say where in Oregon the herd is located or whether it is connected to other infected herds.1 As recently as November 2, Oregon agriculture officials said they had no confirmed or suspected cases in dairy cattle, and the state was listed as unaffected under the federal milk testing program.3 Washington confirmed its first infected dairy herds on October 8.4 The Washington State Department of Agriculture has since confirmed the virus in a Benton County herd that was found through routine surveillance before cows became ill, and Yakima County officials have reported 33 infected herds, according to the Associated Press (AP).2,5 Three people in Washington have been infected after exposure at dairies with infected cattle. One, a Yakima County resident with underlying health conditions, died November 1 after being hospitalized, the first US avian influenza death in a year. A CDC spokesperson told the AP that the agency found no changes in that patient’s virus that would make it spread more easily or cause more severe illness.2 Third new state with a HPAI detection since October Oregon is the third state since early October to report its first infected dairy herd, after Washington and Indiana.4,6 Indiana’s case, confirmed November 2, was found through routine milk testing.6 The dairy cattle outbreak began in March 2024, and APHIS said it has seen cases in previously unaffected states this year.1 Advertisement Federal laboratory testing identified HPAI H5 clade 2.3.4.4b in the Oregon herd, and APHIS said it will announce genetic sequencing results when they are available.1 Sequencing of the first Washington herds, which were tested after cattle showed clinical signs, found H5N1 genotype B3.13, the strain behind most US dairy herd cases. APHIS said those detections were consistent with transmission from Idaho, likely through cattle movement.4,7 APHIS said it is working with the Oregon Department of Agriculture on additional on-farm investigations, diagnostic testing, and epidemiological data collection.1 APHIS said the detection does not change USDA’s HPAI eradication strategy. The agency recommends enhanced biosecurity on all dairy farms and urged producers to report livestock with clinical signs, or unusual sick or dead wildlife, to their state veterinarian.1 “The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is confident that pasteurization is effective at inactivating HPAI virus, and that the commercial, pasteurized milk supply is safe,” APHIS said in an announcement.1 The CDC considers the risk to the general public low, but people with job-related or recreational exposure to infected birds or mammals are at higher risk.1 CDC worker-safety guidance lists veterinarians and veterinary staff among those who may be exposed and recommends high-exposure personal protective equipment for tasks such as contact with potentially infected animals or their raw milk.8 References USDA confirms highly pathogenic avian influenza in a dairy herd in Oregon. news.title_original: Bird flu hits Oregon dairy cattle for the first time as Washington’s infected herds climb into the dozens

analysis.time: The outbreak in Oregon was confirmed on November 12, 2026, with the first detection in dairy cattle. Washington’s infected herds were linked to 3 human infections, including 1 death, as of November 12, 2026. The outbreak in Washington began on October 8, 2026, and the first infected herd was confirmed on that date. The Oregon herd had consistently tested negative before the detection, which occurred weeks after the Washington outbreak.
analysis.location_and_population: The event involves Oregon and Washington states, specifically dairy cattle in Oregon and infected herds in Washington. The outbreak has affected dairy cattle in multiple states, with Washington reporting 33 infected herds. Three people in Washington have been infected after exposure at dairies with infected cattle, including one death in Yakima County.
analysis.event: Bird flu (avian influenza) has been confirmed in an Oregon dairy herd for the first time, making Oregon the 22nd state with infected cattle. This follows the first confirmed cases in Washington’s dairy herds, which were linked to 3 human infections, including 1 death. The outbreak in Washington was confirmed on October 8, 2026, and the Oregon herd was identified through ongoing surveillance.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Three human infections were linked to exposure at dairies, including one death. The CDC considers the risk to the general public low, but people with job-related or recreational exposure to infected birds or mammals are at higher risk. The USDA confirmed the presence of HPAI H5 clade 2.3.4.4b in the Oregon herd and H5N1 genotype B3.13 in Washington’s first herds.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The USDA and APHIS are conducting on-farm investigations, diagnostic testing, and epidemiological data collection. The CDC recommends enhanced biosecurity on dairy farms and high-exposure personal protective equipment for workers handling infected animals or raw milk. The agency also stated that pasteurization is effective at inactivating the HPAI virus, ensuring the commercial milk supply is safe. The detection does not change the USDA’s HPAI eradication strategy.

analysis.brief_en: Bird flu, or avian influenza, has been confirmed in Oregon dairy cattle for the first time, making Oregon the 22nd state with infected herds. This follows the first confirmed cases in Washington’s dairy herds, which were linked to three human infections, including one death. The outbreak in Washington began on October 8, 2026, and the Oregon herd was identified through ongoing surveillance, having tested negative before the detection. The CDC considers the risk to the general public low, but those with exposure to infected animals or raw milk are at higher risk. The USDA confirmed the presence of HPAI H5 clade 2.3.4.4b in Oregon and H5N1 genotype B3.13 in Washington. The agency is conducting investigations and diagnostic testing, emphasizing biosecurity measures and pasteurization as safe for the milk supply. The detection does not alter the USDA’s HPAI eradication strategy.

The outbreak in Washington began on October 8, 2026, and the Oregon herd was identified through ongoing surveillance, having tested negative before the detection. The CDC considers the risk to the general public low, but those with exposure to infected animals or raw milk are at higher risk. The USDA confirmed the presence of HPAI H5 clade 2.3.4.4b in Oregon and H5N1 genotype B3.13 in Washington. The agency is conducting investigations and diagnostic testing, emphasizing biosecurity measures and pasteurization as safe for the milk supply. The detection does not alter the USDA’s HPAI eradication strategy.

elements_zh.time: 俄勒冈州的 暴发 于 2026 年 11 月 12 日得到确认,首次在奶牛中检测到。截至 2026 年 11 月 12 日,华盛顿州受感染的牛群与 3 例人类感染有关,其中 1 例死亡。华盛顿州的 暴发 于 2026 年 10 月 8 日开始,并于该日确认了第一例受感染的牛群。俄勒冈州牛群在检测之前一直呈阴性,而检测发生在华盛顿 暴发 几周后。
elements_zh.location_and_population: 该事件涉及俄勒冈州和华盛顿州,特别是俄勒冈州的奶牛和华盛顿州的受感染牛群。暴发 已影响多个州的奶牛,华盛顿州报告有 33 头奶牛受到感染。华盛顿州已有三人在接触受感染牛的奶牛场后被感染,其中亚基马县有一人死亡。
elements_zh.event: 俄勒冈州的一个奶牛场首次证实存在禽流感(禽流感),使俄勒冈州成为第 22 个有受感染牛的州。在此之前,华盛顿奶牛场出现首例确诊病例,该病例与 3 例人类感染有关,其中 1 例死亡。华盛顿的 暴发 于 2026 年 10 月 8 日得到确认,俄勒冈州的牛群是通过正在进行的 监测 进行识别的。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 三起人类感染事件与乳品店接触有关,其中一人死亡。疾病预防控制中心认为公众面临的风险较低,但因工作或娱乐而接触受感染鸟类或哺乳动物的人面临较高风险。美国农业部确认俄勒冈州牛群中存在 HPAI H5 进化枝 2.3.4.4b,华盛顿州首批牛群中存在 H5N1 基因型 B3.13。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 美国农业部和动植物卫生检验局正在开展农场调查、诊断测试和流行病学数据收集。疾病预防控制中心建议加强奶牛场的生物安全,并为处理受感染动物或原料奶的工人配备高暴露的个人防护装备。该机构还表示,巴氏灭菌可以有效灭活高致病性禽流感病毒,确保商业牛奶供应的安全。此次检测不会改变美国农业部的 HPAI 根除策略。

The outbreak in Washington began on October 8, 2026, and the Oregon herd was identified through ongoing surveillance, having tested negative before the detection. The CDC considers the risk to the general public low, but those with exposure to infected animals or raw milk are at higher risk. The USDA confirmed the presence of HPAI H5 clade 2.3.4.4b in Oregon and H5N1 genotype B3.13 in Washington. The agency is conducting investigations and diagnostic testing, emphasizing biosecurity measures and pasteurization as safe for the milk supply. The detection does not alter the USDA’s HPAI eradication strategy.
news.content_zh: 俄勒冈州奶牛首次确诊禽流感(禽流感),使俄勒冈州成为第 22 个出现感染牛群的州。在此之前,华盛顿奶牛场出现了首例确诊病例,这些病例与三例人类感染有关,其中一人死亡。华盛顿的 暴发 于 2026 年 10 月 8 日开始,俄勒冈州的牛群通过正在进行的 暴发 进行了识别,在检测前检测结果呈阴性。疾病预防控制中心认为公众面临的风险较低,但接触受感染动物或生奶的人面临较高风险。美国农业部确认俄勒冈州存在 HPAI H5 进化枝 2.3.4.4b,华盛顿州存在 H5N1 基因型 B3.13。该机构正在进行调查和诊断测试,强调生物安全措施和巴氏灭菌对于牛奶供应来说是安全的。此次检测不会改变美国农业部的 HPAI 根除策略。

analysis_zh.time: 俄勒冈州的 暴发 于 2026 年 11 月 12 日得到确认,首次在奶牛中检测到。截至 2026 年 11 月 12 日,华盛顿州受感染的牛群与 3 例人类感染有关,其中 1 例死亡。华盛顿州的 暴发 于 2026 年 10 月 8 日开始,并于该日确认了第一例受感染的牛群。俄勒冈州牛群在检测之前一直呈阴性,而检测发生在华盛顿 暴发 几周后。
analysis_zh.location_and_population: 该事件涉及俄勒冈州和华盛顿州,特别是俄勒冈州的奶牛和华盛顿州的受感染牛群。暴发 已影响多个州的奶牛,华盛顿州报告有 33 头奶牛受到感染。华盛顿州已有三人在接触受感染牛的奶牛场后被感染,其中亚基马县有一人死亡。
analysis_zh.event: 俄勒冈州的一个奶牛场首次证实存在禽流感(禽流感),使俄勒冈州成为第 22 个有受感染牛的州。在此之前,华盛顿奶牛场出现首例确诊病例,该病例与 3 例人类感染有关,其中 1 例死亡。华盛顿的 暴发 于 2026 年 10 月 8 日得到确认,俄勒冈州的牛群是通过正在进行的 监测 进行识别的。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 三起人类感染事件与乳品店接触有关,其中一人死亡。疾病预防控制中心认为公众面临的风险较低,但因工作或娱乐而接触受感染鸟类或哺乳动物的人面临较高风险。美国农业部确认俄勒冈州牛群中存在 HPAI H5 进化枝 2.3.4.4b,华盛顿州首批牛群中存在 H5N1 基因型 B3.13。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 美国农业部和动植物卫生检验局正在开展农场调查、诊断测试和流行病学数据收集。疾病预防控制中心建议加强奶牛场的生物安全,并为处理受感染动物或原料奶的工人配备高暴露的个人防护装备。该机构还表示,巴氏灭菌可以有效灭活高致病性禽流感病毒,确保商业牛奶供应的安全。此次检测不会改变美国农业部的 HPAI 根除策略。

analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Two confirmed cases of H5N1 bird flu in England, with no specific case or death counts provided.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Investigation into bird flu risk is ongoing, with a mandatory housing order introduced across England as risk escalates.

analysis.brief_en: Two new cases of H5N1 bird flu have been confirmed in England, according to a report by Poultry News published on November 9, 2026. The outbreak has prompted the introduction of a mandatory housing order across the country to mitigate the risk. While the report highlights the confirmed cases, it does not specify the number of affected animals or human cases. The poultry industry in England is under increased scrutiny, with officials raising the bird flu risk to high for wild birds. The report also notes that the situation is part of a broader context of avian influenza concerns, including recent outbreaks in commercial duck flocks in Lincolnshire and laying flocks in the Scottish Borders. The response includes ongoing investigations and measures to ensure housing standards, but no further details on containment or treatment are provided.

news.title_zh: 英国确诊两例新的 H5N1 禽流感病例 - 家禽新闻
news.source_body_en: Two new cases of H5N1 bird flu have been confirmed in England, according to a report by Poultry News published on November 9, 2026. The outbreak has prompted the introduction of a mandatory housing order across the country to mitigate the risk. While the report highlights the confirmed cases, it does not specify the number of affected animals or human cases. The poultry industry in England is under increased scrutiny, with officials raising the bird flu risk to high for wild birds. The report also notes that the situation is part of a broader context of avian influenza concerns, including recent outbreaks in commercial duck flocks in Lincolnshire and laying flocks in the Scottish Borders. The response includes ongoing investigations and measures to ensure housing standards, but no further details on containment or treatment are provided.
news.content_zh: 据《家禽新闻》2026 年 11 月 9 日发表的报道,英格兰确认了两例新的 H5N1 禽流感病例。暴发 促使在全国范围内引入强制住房令,以降低风险。虽然报告强调了确诊病例,但没有具体说明受影响的动物或人类病例的数量。英格兰的家禽业受到越来越严格的审查,官员们将 野生鸟类 的禽流感风险提高到高水平。报告还指出,这种情况是 禽流感 担忧的更广泛背景的一部分,包括最近林肯郡商业鸭群和苏格兰边境产蛋鸭群中的 暴发。回应包括正在进行的调查和确保住房标准的措施,但没有提供有关遏制或 治疗 的进一步细节。

Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu Oregon logs its first H5N1 case in cows; farmer’s union says human avian flu cases underreported in Washington Stephanie Soucheray, MA Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Diy13/iStock Share Copied to clipboard Earlier this week the US Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (USDA’s APHIS) announced for the first time the detection of H5N1 avian flu in a dairy herd in Oregon. Since 2024, avian flu has been detected in 22 states. Most recently, Washington’s Yakima Valley has reported increased activity. “This detection does not pose a risk to consumer health or affect the safety of the commercial milk supply,” the USDA said. “The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is confident that pasteurization is effective at inactivating HPAI [highly pathogenic avian influenza] virus, and that the commercial, pasteurized milk supply is safe.” According to the USDA, the affected herd was tested as part of Oregon's ongoing surveillance for HPAI in dairy cattle. “Prior to this detection, the herd has consistently tested negative through routine surveillance conducted under the National Milk Testing Strategy program,” the agency said. The USDA said the detection does not change any strategy from the agency and instead emphasized that producers should report any livestock with clinical signs or any unusual sick or dead wildlife to their state veterinarian. Union says H5N1 underreported in Yakima Valley In related news, Union Farm Workers (UFW) posted a statement on X late Tuesday sounding the alarm on human cases of H5N1 in Yakima Valley dairy workers. The union said cases are being widely underreported in part because workers are often immigrants, and there is an ongoing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) surge in Yakima Valley. “UFW staff are trying to support sick workers, but there are many barriers,” the post read. “Workers with milder symptoms are reluctant to be tested or miss work because sick cattle still need care. Workers are very afraid of ICE-related retaliation if they don’t follow employers’ instructions.” Workers are very afraid of ICE-related retaliation if they don’t follow employers’ instructions Earlier this month, a Yakima County resident with underlying health condition died from H5N1, and two others were reported as infected. All case-patients had occupational exposure to dairy cows. The death marked the only US H5N1 death recorded this year and the third recorded since 2024. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there have been 74 human cases of H5N1, including three deaths, in the United States since 2024. The Union said many more workers are sick and are only being offered goggles and gloves for handling raw milk. “The workers report symptoms that range from mild upper respiratory infection with pinkeye to severe flu symptoms with bone pain, severe cough and high fever. We do not have reports that indicate human to human transmission, just workplace exposure to infected animals and milk,” the Union said. In the last 30 days, 51 cattle herds have been hit with H5N1, and in the past week, two herds in Idaho have been identified, as well as the Oregon herd. Washington state has had 43 detections since October 8. news.title_original: Oregon logs its first H5N1 case in cows; farmer’s union says human avian flu cases underreported in Washington

analysis.time: Earlier this week, 2026-11-12.
analysis.location_and_population: Oregon, United States; Yakima Valley, Washington, United States; dairy workers and cattle in the region.
analysis.event: Oregon reported its first H5N1 case in cows, and Yakima Valley in Washington reported increased human H5N1 cases, with one death and two infections, according to the Union Farm Workers (UFW).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: H5N1 has been detected in 22 states since 2024. In Yakima Valley, 51 cattle herds were affected in the last 30 days, and two herds in Idaho were identified in the past week. The USDA confirmed one death in Yakima County from H5N1 and two other infections, with occupational exposure to dairy cows noted. The risk to human health is considered low due to pasteurization, but the UFW claims underreporting due to fear of ICE retaliation.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The USDA emphasized that the detection does not change its strategy and urged producers to report sick livestock. The UFW stated that workers are being offered only basic protective gear, and there are concerns about underreporting due to ICE-related fears. The CDC reported 74 human cases of H5N1 since 2024, including three deaths.

analysis.brief_en: In November 2026, Oregon reported its first case of H5N1 avian flu in a dairy herd, while Yakima Valley in Washington saw increased human H5N1 cases, including one death and two infections. The USDA confirmed the detection in Oregon and stated that pasteurization ensures the safety of the commercial milk supply, posing no risk to consumer health. However, the Union Farm Workers (UFW) highlighted that human cases in Yakima Valley are underreported due to fears of ICE retaliation, with workers experiencing symptoms ranging from mild upper respiratory infections to severe flu-like symptoms. The CDC reported 74 human H5N1 cases since 2024, including three deaths. The USDA urged producers to report any sick livestock, but no changes to its strategy were announced. The outbreak has affected 51 cattle herds in the last 30 days, with two herds in Idaho and the Oregon herd identified in the past week. The UFW also noted that workers are only provided with basic protective gear, raising concerns about safety and reporting practices.
analysis.summary_en: In November 2026, Oregon reported its first case of H5N1 avian flu in a dairy herd, while Yakima Valley in Washington saw increased human H5N1 cases, including one death and two infections. The USDA confirmed the detection in Oregon and stated that pasteurization ensures the safety of the commercial milk supply, posing no risk to consumer health. However, the Union Farm Workers (UFW) highlighted that human cases in Yakima Valley are underreported due to fears of ICE retaliation, with workers experiencing symptoms ranging from mild upper respiratory infections to severe flu-like symptoms. The CDC reported 74 human H5N1 cases since 2024, including three deaths. The USDA urged producers to report any sick livestock, but no changes to its strategy were announced. The outbreak has affected 51 cattle herds in the last 30 days, with two herds in Idaho and the Oregon herd identified in the past week. The UFW also noted that workers are only provided with basic protective gear, raising concerns about safety and reporting practices.

news.title_zh: 禽流感病例随着迁徙而持续 - FarmWeekNow
news.source_body_en: The news report from FarmWeekNow, published on November 11, 2026, highlights the ongoing presence of bird flu cases in the United States, specifically mentioning H5N1 reaching Indiana dairies and poultry cases persisting across the country. The article notes that the situation is continuing with migration, suggesting the spread of the virus may be linked to bird movement. However, the report does not provide specific details on the number of cases, deaths, or exposures, nor does it mention any formal response measures or risk assessments. The information is presented as an update on the current status of avian influenza, with no indication of confirmed or suspected outbreaks beyond the general observation of continued cases. The article is part of a broader discussion on agricultural topics, including weather, harvest, and market trends, which may imply a focus on the impact of the virus on farming operations rather than public health. The content is sourced from FarmWeekNow, a media outlet covering agricultural news, and the report is considered preliminary due to the lack of detailed data on the scale or risk of the outbreak.
news.content_zh: FarmWeekNow 于 2026 年 11 月 11 日发布的新闻报道强调了美国持续存在的禽流感病例,特别提到了 H5N1 到达印第安纳州的乳制品厂和全国各地持续存在的家禽病例。文章指出,这种情况随着迁徙而持续,表明病毒的传播可能与鸟类的迁徙有关。然而,该报告没有提供有关病例、死亡或暴露数量的具体细节,也没有提及任何正式的应对措施或风险评估。该信息作为 禽流感 当前状态的更新提供,除了对持续病例的一般观察之外,没有任何迹象表明确诊或疑似 暴发。这篇文章是有关农业主题的更广泛讨论的一部分,包括天气、收成和市场趋势,这可能意味着重点关注病毒对农业经营的影响,而不是公共卫生。内容来自农业新闻媒体 FarmWeekNow,由于缺乏有关 暴发 规模或风险的详细数据,该报告被认为是初步的。

analysis.time: The USDA confirmed the outbreak on November 11, 2026. The event date is not explicitly stated in the evidence, but the confirmation occurred on that date.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak was confirmed in a dairy herd in Oregon, United States. The affected population includes dairy cattle in Oregon and potentially other states as the virus spreads.
analysis.event: The USDA confirmed the presence of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5 clade 2.3.4.4b in a dairy cattle herd in Oregon. This is a confirmed event based on PCR detection by the National Veterinary Services Laboratories (NVSL).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak has raised concerns about biosecurity and livestock movement as H5N1 bird flu spreads to additional U.S. states, including Washington and Indiana. A Washington resident has died from H5N1 bird flu following dairy cattle exposure. The scale of impact is not fully quantified in the evidence, but the risk is explicitly stated as concerning.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The USDA is conducting genetic sequencing to determine the final results. The response includes ongoing investigation and monitoring of the outbreak, with implications for biosecurity and livestock management.

analysis.brief_en: The USDA confirmed the presence of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5 clade 2.3.4.4b in a dairy cattle herd in Oregon on November 11, 2026, through PCR detection by the National Veterinary Services Laboratories (NVSL). This marks a significant event as the virus spreads to additional U.S. states, including Washington and Indiana, raising concerns about biosecurity and livestock movement. A Washington resident has died from H5N1 bird flu following exposure to dairy cattle, highlighting the potential risk to humans. The USDA is currently conducting genetic sequencing to finalize the results. The outbreak has implications for veterinary practices and animal health management, with ongoing efforts to monitor and contain the spread. The situation remains under investigation, and further details are expected as the genetic analysis is completed.

First Detection of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza in Oregon Dairy Cattle Confirmed Affected dairy under quarantine; milk and food supply remain safe for consumption PUBLISHED ON November 11, 2026 Preliminary detection of HPAI was identified through Oregon's routine statewide milk surveillance program, with preliminary results reported by the Oregon Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory (OVDL) at Oregon State University (OSU) on November 6, 2026. (Photo by David Sjunnesson on Unsplash) SALEM, Ore. — Milk from a Morrow County dairy tested positive for highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI). This is the first detection of HPAI in Oregon dairy cattle. Preliminary detection of HPAI was identified through Oregon‘s routine statewide milk surveillance program, with preliminary results reported by the Oregon Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory (OVDL) at Oregon State University (OSU) on November 6, 2026. The Oregon Department of Agriculture (ODA) immediately initiated an on-farm investigation and submitted additional samples to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) National Veterinary Services Laboratory (NVSL) for confirmation. Positive results were confirmed on November 10, 2026. Oregon’s routine statewide milk surveillance program identified the detection, demonstrating the effectiveness of the state’s ongoing monitoring efforts. No additional affected dairies have been identified at this time. Pasteurized milk and dairy products remain safe to consume, and there is no concern about the safety of the commercial milk supply. Pasteurization effectively inactivates the HPAI virus, and milk from sick animals is prohibited from entering the commercial milk supply. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) continues to advise against consuming raw (unpasteurized) milk because it does not undergo the heating process that kills viruses and bacteria. “While this detection is significant, it is not unexpected given the continued spread of HPAI among dairy cattle nationally,” said Dr. Ryan Scholz, State Veterinarian for ODA. “Oregon‘s milk surveillance program worked exactly as intended, identifying this infection quickly and allowing us to respond rapidly with our state and federal partners. This detection demonstrates the value of the monitoring and preparedness efforts supported by Oregon‘s dairy industry and animal health partners since 2024.” ODA has placed the affected dairy under quarantine, and enhanced biosecurity measures are in place. The quarantine restricts animal movement and implements additional disease control measures while response activities are conducted. Response activities are focused on the impacted dairy and associated epidemiologic investigation. In most cases, infected dairy cows are expected to recover within a few weeks. ODA is coordinating closely with USDA, Oregon Health Authority (OHA) and Morrow County Public Health officials, OVDL, and Oregon‘s dairy industry partners as the investigation continues. Oregon‘s statewide dairy surveillance program, launched in December 2024, was established to detect HPAI early and support rapid response efforts. The program allows state and federal officials to implement disease control measures quickly when detections occur. Public health officials are providing education to farm workers exposed to infected animals and will monitor them for symptoms of avian influenza throughout the outbreak. “With the use of appropriate personal protective equipment, the risk to farm workers remains low. Our public health approach is focused on ensuring rapid testing and treatment for any individuals who develop symptoms to prevent severe disease,” said Melissa Sutton, M.D., medical director, respiratory viral pathogens, OHA. No human cases associated with this incident have been identified in Oregon. According to OHA and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the current public health risk to the general population remains low. No cases of person-to-person transmission associated with this virus have been identified. HPAI was first detected in U.S. dairy cattle in March 2024 and has since been identified in multiple states. USDA provides current information on HPAI detections in livestock. Oregon began statewide dairy milk surveillance in December 2024 and continues to test milk from all licensed dairy operations routinely. ODA appreciates the cooperation of Oregon dairy producers and industry partners who participate in ongoing surveillance, disease reporting, and biosecurity efforts that help protect animal health and Oregon‘s dairy industry. Symptoms of HPAI in Dairy Cattle Symptoms can include: Decrease in feed consumption with a simultaneous decrease in rumination and rumen motility. Respiratory signs, including clear nasal discharge. Acute drop in milk production. Abnormal tacky or loose feces. Lethargy. Dehydration. Fever. Thicker, more concentrated, colostrum-like milk, or no milk production in severely affected animals. Some infected cattle may show no clinical signs. Most infected cattle recover within two to three weeks. Suspected cases of HPAI in any animal species should be reported immediately to ODA at 503-986-4711. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 13, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Baloxavir and Molnupiravir Protect Immunosuppressed Hamsters Against Severe Avian Influenza by November 11, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Baloxavir and Molnupiravir Protect Immunosuppressed Hamsters Against Severe Avian Influenza Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers investigating therapeutic options for avian influenza have found that the antiviral drugs baloxavir and high-dose molnupiravir effectively protected immunocompromised hamsters from lethal infection with a human isolate of influenza A(H5N1). Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) viruses have continued to expand their geographic and animal host ranges, intensifying concerns regarding zoonotic transmission events and general pandemic preparedness. While immunocompromised individuals face elevated risks of developing severe, prolonged disease when infected by these emerging viruses, experimental evidence guiding clinical antiviral selection has remained scarce. To evaluate disease development and antiviral treatments, the research team characterized viral pathogenesis and assessed direct-contact transmission using an influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b genotype D1.1 virus strain. This specific viral isolate was recently obtained from an infected human case in British Columbia, Canada. Investigators established an animal model using hamsters immunosuppressed with cyclophosphamide and included normal hamsters to compare clinical infection outcomes, survival benchmarks, and viral shedding kinetics over the infection course. Discover more Engineering job board Research publication platform Scientific instrument sales The baseline experiments revealed clear contrasts between normal animals and immunosuppressed subjects. Normal hamsters experienced no mortality and successfully achieved complete viral clearance following exposure to the Canadian avian influenza isolate. In stark contrast, infection among the cyclophosphamide-treated immunosuppressed hamsters produced severe clinical illness marked by prolonged viral replication, viral invasion into the brain, and a 75 percent mortality rate. In addition, the research team detected no direct-contact viral transmission between the infected hamsters and uninfected contacts during these transmission evaluations. Discover more Get Cold Relief Check Symptoms Save on Rx Read Med Journals In subsequent therapeutic trials, investigators evaluated three distinct antiviral compounds administered as monotherapies or in dual combinations across the immunosuppressed cohort. Treatment protocols tested oseltamivir at 20 mg/kg twice daily for five days, baloxavir at 50 mg/kg given in two doses, and molnupiravir administered twice daily at either a low dose of 50 mg/kg or a high dose of 200 mg/kg. The team also evaluated a combination regimen pairing standard oseltamivir with low-dose molnupiravir, while maintaining an untreated placebo group for controlled comparison. The efficacy evaluations demonstrated striking differences across the therapeutic regimens compared with the placebo control, where infected hamsters exhibited 50 percent mortality. Baloxavir monotherapy resulted in 100 percent survival, shortened the duration of viral shedding, curtailed viral replication, lessened pulmonary inflammatory responses, and completely prevented neuroinvasion. High-dose molnupiravir at 200 mg/kg likewise prevented mortality and successfully achieved viral clearance in both lung and brain tissues. The combination of oseltamivir and low-dose molnupiravir yielded 75 percent survival, reduced morbidity relative to either monotherapy, and also accomplished viral clearance in both lung and brain tissues. By contrast, oseltamivir monotherapy produced 75 percent survival but failed to prevent severe clinical signs or reduce viral titers in target tissues, while low-dose molnupiravir monotherapy resulted in outcomes comparable to placebo. Together, these experimental findings indicate that human A(H5N1) isolates can cause severe and invasive pathology in immunocompromised hosts, while demonstrating that baloxavir and molnupiravir-based regimens offer effective therapeutic options. analysis.time: The study was published on November 11, 2026. The experiments were conducted using a viral isolate obtained from a human case in British Columbia, Canada, and the results were reported on the same date.
analysis.location_and_population: The research was conducted in an unspecified location, but the viral isolate used in the study was obtained from a human case in British Columbia, Canada. analysis.event: Researchers tested the antiviral drugs baloxavir and molnupiravir for their efficacy in protecting immunosuppressed hamsters from severe avian influenza A(H5N1) infection. The study found that these drugs significantly reduced mortality and viral replication in immunocompromised hosts, while normal hamsters showed no mortality and complete viral clearance.

analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was conducted in a controlled experimental setting, with treatment protocols tested on immunosuppressed hamsters. Baloxavir monotherapy resulted in 100% survival, reduced viral shedding, and prevented neuroinvasion. High-dose molnupiravir also achieved 100% survival and viral clearance in both lung and brain tissues. The study highlights the heightened risk of severe disease in immunocompromised individuals and suggests that baloxavir and molnupiravir-based regimens may offer effective therapeutic options. These findings are based on experimental models and are not yet applicable to human populations, though they contribute to pandemic preparedness and antiviral therapy research.

news.title_zh: Baloxavir 和 Molnupiravir 保护免疫抑制仓鼠免受严重 禽流感 - Bioengineer.org
news.source_body_en: A study published on November 11, 2026, by Bioengineer.org investigated the effectiveness of antiviral drugs baloxavir and molnupiravir in protecting immunosuppressed hamsters from severe avian influenza A(H5N1) infection. The research used a viral isolate obtained from a human case in British Columbia, Canada, and tested these drugs against immunocompromised hamsters treated with cyclophosphamide. Normal hamsters showed no mortality and complete viral clearance, while immunosuppressed hamsters had a 75% mortality rate without treatment. Baloxavir monotherapy resulted in 100% survival, reduced viral shedding, and prevented neuroinvasion. High-dose molnupiravir also achieved 100% survival and viral clearance in both lung and brain tissues. The study highlights the heightened risk of severe disease in immunocompromised individuals and suggests that baloxavir and molnupiravir-based regimens may offer effective therapeutic options. These findings are based on experimental models and are not yet applicable to human populations, though they contribute to pandemic preparedness and antiviral therapy research.

The girl reported symptom onset on October 13, and the boy on September 20. Mainland China has now recorded 23 H9N2 cases in the past six months. Of those cases, all but six occurred in children. The World Health Organization (WHO) has tracked 189 cases of human infection with H9N2 since 2015, including two deaths in patients with underlying health conditions. Most cases are mild to moderate in severity, with people typically exposed to infected poultry in their homes of communities. “Current evidence indicates that H9N2 viruses have not acquired the ability for sustained human-to-human transmission, and the risk of further community-level spread remains low,” the WHO said. CDC declares its probe into outbreak of E coli, Salmonella illnesses tied to alfalfa sprouts over News brief Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics E coli Foodborne Disease Salmonella Jovan J / Flickr cc The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said yesterday that a multistate outbreak of Escherichia coli and Salmonella infections linked to tainted alfalfa sprouts is now over, after sickening at least 77 people. The case count represents one new infection since the most recent update on October 1. Of the 77 case-patients, three were sickened with both pathogens, 10 with Salmonella, and 64 with E coli. Cases were reported in 16 states, and six patients were hospitalized for their illnesses. No deaths were reported. Illness onset ranged from May 31 to October 16 of this year. Alfalfa, radish sprouts and seeds recalled “The true number of sick people in this outbreak was likely much higher than the number reported, and this outbreak may not have been limited to the states with known illnesses,” the CDC said. PulseNet first identified this outbreak in July 2026, and in August, Everything Sprouts, LLC recalled certain lots of sprouts sold under the Calco and Everything Sprouts brands at retailers and grocery stores, according to the CDC. In addition to alfalfa sprouts, radish sprouts and alfalfa sprout seeds were also eventually recalled. Some cases occurred in clusters, with Minnesota and Wisconsin reporting the most cases with 29 and 27, respectively. analysis.time: Two new H9N2 avian flu cases were reported in China, with symptom onset on October 13 and September 20, respectively. The CDC's probe into E. coli and Salmonella illnesses tied to alfalfa sprouts was declared over yesterday, and the outbreak was first identified in July 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The cases occurred in Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region and Liaoning province, China. Mainland China has recorded 23 H9N2 cases in the past six months, with all but six cases occurring in children.
analysis.event: The World Health Organization (WHO) reported two new H9N2 avian flu cases in children in China. The CDC confirmed the end of a multistate outbreak of E. coli and Salmonella infections linked to tainted alfalfa sprouts.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The WHO noted that H9N2 viruses have not acquired sustained human-to-human transmission and the risk of further community-level spread remains low.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC declared the outbreak over, and PulseNet first identified the outbreak in July 2026. Some cases occurred in clusters, with Minnesota and Wisconsin reporting the most cases. The true number of sick people may be higher than reported.

analysis.brief_en: In China, two new H9N2 avian flu cases were confirmed, involving a 9-year-old girl in Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region and a 7-year-old boy from Liaoning province. The girl showed symptoms on October 13, while the boy's onset was on September 20. These cases are part of a broader trend, as mainland China has recorded 23 H9N2 cases in the past six months, with all but six occurring in children. The World Health Organization (WHO) stated that H9N2 viruses have not acquired the ability for sustained human-to-human transmission, and the risk of further community-level spread remains low. The CDC confirmed the end of a multistate outbreak of E. coli and Salmonella infections linked to tainted alfalfa sprouts, which was first identified in July 2026. The outbreak involved 77 cases, with three patients infected with both pathogens, 10 with Salmonella, and 64 with E. coli. Cases were reported in 16 states, and six patients were hospitalized, though no deaths were reported. Why is public risk from bird flu considered low? topics: Bird flu Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza Snohomish County Lake Tye Park Dead birds Public health Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife Wildlife MONROE, Wash. — Dead birds found at Lake Tye Park in Monroe have preliminarily tested positive for Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, also known as bird flu, the Snohomish County Health Department said. Health officials said the virus circulates naturally among birds and can cause severe illness and high death rates in chickens, turkey, geese and ducks. SEE ALSO | Western Washington farmers brace for impacts after bird flu detected in Pierce County The risk to the general public is low and transmission to humans is uncommon, but people with direct exposure to infected birds - including backyard flock owners or those handling sick or dead birds - are at higher risk. The Health Department said two workers from the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife picked up dead birds at Lake Tye wearing appropriate personal protective equipment, following agency and veterinary guidance and standing guidance from health officials. Powered By 10 Sec Race for state representative seat in Pierce County separated by 4 votes Next Stay The workers will self-monitor for possible symptoms of illness caused by avian influenza. At this time, the Health Department said there is no evidence of broader community risk, and it is not aware of any other cases of HPAI in Snohomish County. The Washington State Department of Health has information on its website about what to do if you see birds suspected of being ill and how to protect yourself. The state also tracks detections on the Washington State Avian Influenza Outbreak Map. Health officials urged people to report signs of illness in domestic flocks. If a flock experiences sudden death or illness of multiple birds, people should call the Washington State Department of Agriculture Sick Bird Hotline at (800) 606-3056 or use the agency’s online reporting tool. If birds have died, officials said to double-bag the carcasses and keep them in a cooler with ice until WSDA can arrange for sampling. They also advised people not to allow scavenger birds to access carcasses because it can spread the virus. analysis.brief_en: In Snohomish County, Washington, dead birds found at Lake Tye Park in Monroe have preliminarily tested positive for Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI), also known as bird flu, according to the Snohomish County Health Department. The virus circulates naturally among birds and can cause severe illness and high death rates in chickens, turkeys, geese, and ducks. Health officials emphasized that the risk to the general public is low, as transmission to humans is uncommon. However, individuals with direct exposure to infected birds, such as backyard flock owners or those handling sick or dead birds, are at higher risk. The Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife workers collected the birds wearing appropriate personal protective equipment, following agency and veterinary guidance. They will self-monitor for possible symptoms of avian influenza. The Health Department stated there is no evidence of broader community risk and is not aware of any other HPAI cases in the county. Officials urged people to report signs of illness in domestic flocks and advised against allowing scavenger birds to access carcasses to prevent the spread of the virus.

news.content_zh: 据斯诺霍米什县卫生局称,在华盛顿州斯诺霍米什县,门罗泰伊湖公园发现的死鸟初步检测出 高致病性禽流感 (HPAI)(也称为禽流感)呈阳性。该病毒在鸟类中自然传播,可导致鸡、火鸡、鹅和鸭的严重疾病和高死亡率。卫生官员强调,由于 传播 对人类的影响并不常见,因此公众面临的风险较低。然而,直接接触受感染鸟类的个人,例如后院鸡群的主人或处理病鸟或死鸟的人,风险较高。华盛顿鱼类和野生动物部门的工作人员按照机构和兽医的指导,穿着适当的个人防护装备收集了这些鸟类。他们将自我监测 禽流感 可能的症状。卫生部门表示,没有证据表明存在更广泛的社区风险,并且不知道该县有任何其他高致病性禽流感病例。官员们敦促人们报告家禽鸡群的疾病迹象,并建议不要让食腐鸟接触尸体,以防止病毒传播。

The Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) said highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 had been discovered in commercial poultry at premises near Dersingham. A 1.86-mile (3km) protection zone and a 6.21-mile (10km) surveillance zone have been put in place around the site. All poultry on the premises will be humanely culled, APHA said. The restrictions mean all bird keepers must follow stringent biosecurity measures in addition to the protection and surveillance measures. The number of cases of bird flu in the UK so far this autumn now stands at five. According to APHA, the protective zone means there are restrictions on the movement of birds and eggs and restrictions on people coming into contact with poultry and poultry eggs. Transmission from birds to humans is rare, and there has been no sustained human-to-human transmission. According to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the risk to the general public's health posed by avian influenza remained very low, while the Food Standards Agency (FSA) said it posed a very low food safety risk, with properly cooked poultry and poultry products, including eggs, safe to eat. You cannot vaccinate poultry or most captive birds against bird flu in England. APHA Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? Contact us below. news.source_body_en: A confirmed case of bird flu (H5N1) has been identified at commercial poultry premises near Dersingham in Norfolk, UK. This marks the first occurrence of the virus in Norfolk this autumn, raising the total number of cases in the UK to five. The Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) confirmed the outbreak, and all poultry on the site will be humanely culled. A 1.86-mile (3km) protection zone and a 6.21-mile (10km) surveillance zone have been established around the site. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) stated that the risk to public health remains very low, with no sustained human-to-human transmission reported. Properly cooked poultry and eggs are considered safe for consumption. Bird keepers are required to follow strict biosecurity measures. The response is based on confirmed evidence and official guidelines, with no indication of broader public health risks.

analysis.event: State agricultural directors are urging the USDA to develop a bird flu vaccine for cattle, as the virus has been confirmed in Idaho poultry operations and is suspected to have spread to Washington dairy herds. The bird flu outbreak in Idaho was confirmed by USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The bird flu outbreak in Idaho affected about 10,000 birds, and it is suspected that the virus spread to Washington dairy herds. The USDA has not yet provided a vaccine for cattle, and the risk of further spread is a concern for the dairy industry.

news.title: Oregon agriculture officials confirm state’s first case of bird flu in dairy cattle
news.excerpt: Up until now, bird flu’s effect on agriculture in the state has mostly impacted commercial and backyard chickens.

news.content_title: Oregon agriculture officials confirm state’s first case of bird flu in dairy cattle
news.content: Independent. Member-supported. For the Pacific Northwest. Independent. Member-supported. donate now Oregon agriculture officials confirm state’s first case of bird flu in dairy cattle By Alejandro Figueroa (OPB) Portland, Ore. Nov. 12, 2026 11:03 p.m. Up until now, bird flu’s effect on agriculture in the state has mostly impacted commercial and backyard chickens. For the first time, bird flu has been detected on a commercial dairy farm in Oregon. On Tuesday, the Oregon Department of Agriculture confirmed a positive test result for the virus, known as highly pathogenic avian influenza, at a Morrow County dairy. State agriculture officials have not identified any other affected dairies as of Thursday. THANKS TO OUR SPONSOR: Become a Sponsor Oregon agriculture officials say they’ve put the Morrow County farm under quarantine and will continue to investigate how the cows got sick. FILE - A cow stands in a field at the U.S. Department of Agriculture's National Animal Disease Center research facility in Ames, Iowa, on Tuesday, Aug. 6, 2024. Charlie Neibergall / AP Earlier this month, a farmworker in Washington’s Yakima County died after contracting the virus, though human deaths linked to bird flu are very rare. Health officials in that state say that the dairy worker had underlying health conditions. Two Yakima farmworkers also contracted the virus but did not experience severe illness, nor were they hospitalized. Officials maintain the nation’s milk supply and other dairy products are safe to consume since pasteurization effectively inactivates the virus. Milk from sick animals is also diverted or destroyed so that it does not enter the food supply. The current public health risk to the general population remains low, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, although people working in close contact with dairy cattle or poultry are at a higher risk of getting sick. While the Oregon detection is significant, it’s not surprising, said Dr. Ryan Scholz, the state veterinarian for the Oregon Department of Agriculture. The virus is spreading among dairy cattle across the country, he said. THANKS TO OUR SPONSOR: Become a Sponsor “Oregon’s milk surveillance program worked exactly as intended, identifying this infection quickly and allowing us to respond rapidly with our state and federal partners,” Scholz said in a statement. Bird flu was first detected in dairy cattle in March 2024 and has since been identified in multiple states, including Washington, Idaho and California. Oregon officials first discovered the virus in Morrow County through the state Department of Agriculture’s routine statewide milk surveillance program, which began weekly testing in late 2024. Oregon health officials did not immediately disclose how many people were exposed to the sick cows in Morrow County. But they are monitoring farmworkers exposed to the infected animals and will keep checking them for symptoms, said Dr. Melissa Sutton, the medical director of respiratory viral pathogens at the Oregon Health Authority. “With the use of appropriate personal protective equipment, the risk to farm workers remains low,” Sutton said in a statement. “Our public health approach is focused on ensuring rapid testing and treatment for any individuals who develop symptoms to prevent severe disease.” In Washington, the virus has spread rapidly with at least 41 dairy farms testing positive for bird flu over the last 30 days. This is the same virus that has affected millions of poultry birds across the U.S. since 2022, including more than one million commercial and backyard chickens in Oregon, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Of all known bird flu infections in Oregon, most have been on commercial poultry farms and backyard flocks. There is evidence that suggests the virus affecting dairy cattle is mainly spreading from cow to cow, unlike in commercial or backyard poultry farms. Poultry usually catch the virus from wild migratory waterfowl. Unlike what the name suggests, avian flu can jump to other animals, including wild mammals. In Oregon the virus has been detected in at least one pig at a noncommercial farm, in skunks, raccoons, rodents and at least five cats last year. Apps and Podcasts Community Calendar Meet The Team Contests Jobs What’s On Case of avian influenza detected in Worcester County November 11, 2026 Sophia Peters, WORCESTER COUNTY, Md. – The Maryland Department of Agriculture (MDA) has announced the detection highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza in Worcester County. Officials say, following routine surveillance, poultry at the affected commercial broiler operation preliminarily tested positive for the virus, also known as “bird flu”. As a result, the affected property has been placed under quarantine. The flock is being depopulated to prevent further spread of the disease, and birds from the affected flock will not enter the food supply chain. The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Veterinary Services Laboratories is currently testing to confirm the disease, with final results expected in the coming days. “It is critical that all commercial growers and backyard flock owners maintain strict biosecurity protocols and report any signs of illness immediately,” said MDA Secretary Kevin Atticks. “Our department, along with our state and federal partners, is monitoring the situation closely to protect Maryland’s agricultural community.” Avian influenza is a highly contagious respiratory virus that spreads rapidly among birds through nasal secretions, saliva and manure. The virus can easily travel between flocks via wild birds, contact with infected poultry, or on contaminated equipment, clothing and footwear. It affects domestic poultry including chickens, ducks and turkeys, as well as wild bird species such as geese, shorebirds and raptors. Risk of transmission to the general public remains low. For more information on avian influenza, visit MDA’s website here. The MDA’s National Veterinary Services Laboratories are conducting tests to confirm the disease, with final results expected soon. Officials emphasize the importance of maintaining strict biosecurity protocols and promptly reporting any signs of illness to protect Maryland’s agricultural community. The risk of transmission to the general public remains low, and the MDA is collaborating with state and federal partners to monitor the situation closely.
