Tennessee project offers answers By AGDAILY Contributors Read More Read Tickborne meat allergy poses challenges for farmers Read Penn State study finds most soil microbes stay dormant after rainfall Read 3 farm dogs compete for AFBF People’s Choice Pup honors Agriculture news Nov 12, 2026 Livestock Read AGDAILY H5N1 jumps from Illinois backyard flock to cat and rats An outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza that nearly destroyed an Illinois farmer’s backyard birds also infected a cat and wild rats on the farm, according to an analysis by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory and the University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Laboratory. The case points to rodents as a potentially overlooked bridge for the virus to move between wild birds, poultry, and other mammals. In March 2025, the farmer lost 100 of his 105 backyard birds and took the remains of five birds and a rat to the University of Missouri. The farm sat about two miles from a reservoir lake, positioning it for the virus to reach the flock from wild waterfowl. A sample from one chicken tested positive for avian influenza. Four days afterward, the farm’s primary veterinarian sent the carcasses of a cat and a second rat to the University of Illinois lab, as there had been reports of infections in cats at the time. Both mammals carried the same H5N1 subtype identified in the chicken. Tissue testing found all 12 cat samples infected, along with 11 of 15 rat samples, and viral RNA also turned up in the rat’s urine. “The cat was expected, but the rat is the surprise,” said Dr. Leyi Wang, who heads the virology section at the U. of I. Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory and serves as a professor of veterinary clinical medicine. “Since rats live on nearly every farm despite biosecurity, they may be an overlooked link between wild birds, poultry and other mammals.”= Sequencing of the viral genomes from the chicken, cat, and rat showed nearly identical sequences, indicating spillover from the poultry to the two mammals. All three carried a mutation that better equips the avian virus to infect mammals. “Because the mammalian-adaptation marker was already present in the bird virus, crossing into mammals may not require new mutations,” Wang said. Wang urged flock owners to keep poultry away from wild waterfowl, report sudden die-offs, control rodents, and prevent farm cats from scavenging dead birds. The findings were published in the CDC journal Emerging Infectious Diseases. This article was prepared with the assistance of automated tools and human research and verified by our editorial team. Share Nov 12, 2026 Crops Read AGDAILY About 275 gallons of diesel stolen from field equipment Approximately 275 gallons of diesel fuel were allegedly stolen from a tractor and combine parked in a Blackford County, Indiana, field overnight, prompting the sheriff’s office to warn farmers about securing equipment left unattended during harvest. According to the Blackford County Sheriff’s Office, the theft was discovered Wednesday morning after someone reportedly drained fuel from both machines parked along East County Road 600 North near the 5200 block. Based on recent agricultural diesel prices of approximately $5.50 to $5.75 per gallon, the stolen fuel could be worth more than $1,500. Beyond the cost of replacing the fuel, thefts can leave farmers facing equipment downtime during an already busy harvest season. No suspects or arrests have been announced, and the investigation remains ongoing. The sheriff’s office is encouraging farmers to remain vigilant when leaving tractors, combines, and other equipment in fields overnight. Large fuel tanks and remote locations can make unattended machinery attractive targets for thieves. Farmers can help reduce the risk of fuel theft by using locking fuel caps, installing security or trail cameras, and parking equipment in visible or well-lit locations when possible. Investigators are asking anyone with security camera footage from the area to come forward. They are also interested in information about anyone who may have recently obtained an unusually large quantity of diesel fuel under suspicious circumstances. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Blackford County Sheriff’s Office at 765-348-0930. This article was prepared with the assistance of automated tools and human research and verified by our editorial team. Share Nov 12, 2026 Read AGDAILY Reporters Tickborne meat allergy poses challenges for farmers The first peer-reviewed study examining alpha-gal syndrome among farmers and ranchers found that those living with the tickborne red meat allergy averaged three medical visits before receiving a diagnosis, with some reporting more than 10 visits. Published in the Journal of Agromedicine, the study surveyed 201 farmers and ranchers across 26 states, making it the first research of its kind to focus specifically on how the condition affects agricultural producers. Researchers identified four distinct symptom patterns and found that symptoms differed between men and women. General practitioners and allergists were responsible for most diagnoses, but patients experiencing severe symptoms typically required more medical visits. The findings highlight a growing concern for agricultural workers, whose daily exposure to pastures, livestock and wooded areas puts them at greater risk for tick bites. Alpha-gal syndrome is a potentially serious allergy associated with tick bites, particularly those from the lone star tick. The condition causes reactions to a sugar molecule found in most mammalian meat and certain animal-derived products, including some dairy products and medications. Unlike typical food allergies, symptoms may not appear until three to six hours after exposure, making it difficult for patients to connect their reactions to something they ate. Symptoms vary widely among farmers and ranchers Researchers identified four distinct symptom patterns among participants: severe, gastrointestinal, mild and allergy-related. The most frequently reported symptoms included abdominal cramping, diarrhea, itchy skin and nausea. Other participants experienced hives, rashes, difficulty breathing and swelling. Women were more likely to report gastrointestinal symptoms, while men were more frequently represented in the mild symptom group. More than 85 percent of respondents experienced symptoms daily or weekly, yet only about half initially suspected their symptoms were related to food. Despite working in environments where tick exposure is common, fewer than half of participants, 46.8 percent, were familiar with alpha-gal syndrome before their diagnosis. The survey also found that 77 percent recalled being bitten by a tick, while 87 percent reported experiencing multiple bites. Nearly all respondents, 95 percent, said they regularly checked themselves for ticks. Getting a diagnosis can be difficult Participants averaged 2.98 medical visits before receiving a diagnosis, although some reported 10 or more visits. Those experiencing primarily allergy-related symptoms received diagnoses more quickly, averaging 2.25 visits. Participants with severe symptoms averaged 4.03 visits. General practitioners and allergists accounted for most diagnoses, with each responsible for roughly one-third of cases. Researchers noted that additional appointments can be particularly burdensome for agricultural workers, who may already face long drives to medical facilities, limited access to specialists and difficulty leaving their operations. The study also referenced previous research finding that 42 percent of surveyed health care providers had never heard of alpha-gal syndrome, highlighting the continued need for education in rural medical communities. Image by BY-_-BY, Shutterstock The implications extend beyond personal health. Farmers and ranchers may face continued tick exposure through everyday activities such as checking livestock, repairing fences, managing pastures and working in wooded or brush-covered areas. Alpha-gal syndrome can also complicate dietary choices and potentially affect exposure to certain animal-derived products. Researchers emphasized that the condition’s wide range of symptoms makes awareness especially important. Patients experiencing gastrointestinal problems may not recognize the possibility of an allergic reaction, particularly when symptoms develop hours after eating. The study has limitations, including recruitment primarily through social media and reliance on self-reported diagnoses that were not independently verified. The findings do not establish how common alpha-gal syndrome is among agricultural workers, but they highlight the challenges facing those who develop the condition. As tick populations expand into new geographic areas, researchers say improving awareness among agricultural workers and rural health care providers will be important for recognizing symptoms and reducing delays in diagnosis. Share Nov 12, 2026 Crops Read AGDAILY Reporters Penn State study finds most soil microbes stay dormant after rainfall Rainfall may bring much-needed moisture to dryland soils, but new research from Penn State University suggests that most of the microorganisms living beneath the surface don’t immediately respond when water arrives. Researchers studying biological soil crusts, commonly called biocrusts, found that only a small fraction of bacteria became active within six hours of rainfall. The findings could help scientists develop more effective ways to restore fragile soils in arid and semi-arid regions. Biocrusts are communities of cyanobacteria, algae, lichens, mosses and other microorganisms that form a thin layer across the soil surface. These living crusts play an important role in dryland ecosystems, helping stabilize soil and supporting biological processes in environments where water is scarce. However, researchers warn that biocrust ecosystems are increasingly threatened, with projections suggesting they could decline by as much as 40 percent over the next 45 years. The study, published in The ISME Journal, examined how microbial communities respond when dry soil receives moisture after extended periods without rainfall. Researchers collected biocrust samples near Moab, Utah, in the Colorado Plateau, where annual precipitation averages less than 10 inches. The samples were transported to Penn State and studied under controlled conditions that simulated rainfall during both daytime and nighttime. Image by Meryll, Shutterstock Using molecular techniques to identify bacteria actively producing proteins, the team discovered that most microorganisms remained dormant even after moisture became available. More mature biocrusts had a greater proportion of active microbes than younger, less-developed crusts. The researchers also found that the most abundant bacteria weren’t necessarily the ones that responded to rainfall. Surprisingly, whether rainfall occurred during daylight or nighttime had little effect on microbial activity during the first six hours. “Because biocrusts are supported by photosynthetic microbes, we expected them to have a very different response when the rain fell at night when they could not do photosynthesis versus during the day,” said Raúl Román, the study’s first author. “But we did not find that.” The findings suggest that understanding which microorganisms are present in soil may be less important than identifying which ones become active when conditions change. “Our results suggest that across these communities there is a relatively conserved group of microbes that are especially good at rapidly responding when water becomes available,” said Estelle Couradeau, Penn State assistant professor of soils and environmental microbiology. “Simply knowing which microbes are present may not tell us how the soil will function after rainfall. If we are to effectively restore biocrusts, we need to know which microbes actually activate when precipitation occurs — especially as climate change alters the timing and size of rainfall events. Photo by Tanja Esser, Shutterstock What the findings mean for dryland restoration The research could have implications for soil restoration efforts in drought-prone regions, where biological soil crusts contribute to ecosystem stability. By identifying microorganisms that respond quickly to moisture, scientists hope to eventually cultivate beneficial microbes that could be used to help restore damaged biocrust communities. “Biocrust microbial communities are able to maintain metabolic activity when it’s wet and then turn to quiescence or dormancy when it’s dry for a long period,” Román said. “That’s a very important advantage that allows them to colonize these harsh, barren areas. But we think with more research, we can isolate microbes that are active, and then culture them, and use them for restoration.” The work remains in the research stage, and the study did not evaluate microbial restoration treatments in agricultural fields. Still, understanding how these organisms respond to rainfall could help researchers better predict how dryland ecosystems will function as precipitation patterns change. For regions facing longer droughts or increasingly unpredictable rainfall, the findings offer another piece of the puzzle in understanding how soil ecosystems survive under difficult conditions. The findings do not establish how common alpha-gal syndrome is among agricultural workers, but they highlight the challenges facing those who develop the condition. As tick populations expand into new geographic areas, researchers say improving awareness among agricultural workers and rural health care providers will be important for recognizing symptoms and reducing delays in diagnosis. Share Nov 12, 2026 Crops Read AGDAILY Reporters Penn State study finds most soil microbes stay dormant after rainfall Rainfall may bring much-needed moisture to dryland soils, but new research from Penn State University suggests that most of the microorganisms living beneath the surface don’t immediately respond when water arrives. Researchers studying biological soil crusts, commonly called biocrusts, found that only a small fraction of bacteria became active within six hours of rainfall. The findings could help scientists develop more effective ways to restore fragile soils in arid and semi-arid regions. Biocrusts are communities of cyanobacteria, algae, lichens, mosses and other microorganisms that form a thin layer across the soil surface. These living crusts play an important role in dryland ecosystems, helping stabilize soil and supporting biological processes in environments where water is scarce. However, researchers warn that biocrust ecosystems are increasingly threatened, with projections suggesting they could decline by as much as 40 percent over the next 45 years. The study, published in The ISME Journal, examined how microbial communities respond when dry soil receives moisture after extended periods without rainfall. Researchers collected biocrust samples near Moab, Utah, in the Colorado Plateau, where annual precipitation averages less than 10 inches. The samples were transported to Penn State and studied under controlled conditions that simulated rainfall during both daytime and nighttime. Image by Meryll, Shutterstock Using molecular techniques to identify bacteria actively producing proteins, the team discovered that most microorganisms remained dormant even after moisture became available. More mature biocrusts had a greater proportion of active microbes than younger, less-developed crusts. The researchers also found that the most abundant bacteria weren’t necessarily the ones that responded to rainfall. Surprisingly, whether rainfall occurred during daylight or nighttime had little effect on microbial activity during the first six hours. “Because biocrusts are supported by photosynthetic microbes, we expected them to have a very different response when the rain fell at night when they could not do photosynthesis versus during the day,” said Raúl Román, the study’s first author. “But we did not find that.” The findings suggest that understanding which microorganisms are present in soil may be less important than identifying which ones become active when conditions change. “Our results suggest that across these communities there is a relatively conserved group of microbes that are especially good at rapidly responding when water becomes available,” said Estelle Couradeau, Penn State assistant professor of soils and environmental microbiology. “Simply knowing which microbes are present may not tell us how the soil will function after rainfall. If we are to effectively restore biocrusts, we need to know which microbes actually activate when precipitation occurs — especially as climate change alters the timing and size of rainfall events. Photo by Tanja Esser, Shutterstock What the findings mean for dryland restoration The research could have implications for soil restoration efforts in drought-prone regions, where biological soil crusts contribute to ecosystem stability. By identifying microorganisms that respond quickly to moisture, scientists hope to eventually cultivate beneficial microbes that could be used to help restore damaged biocrust communities. “Biocrust microbial communities are able to maintain metabolic activity when it’s wet and then turn to quiescence or dormancy when it’s dry for a long period,” Román said. “That’s a very important advantage that allows them to colonize these harsh, barren areas. But we think with more research, we can isolate microbes that are active, and then culture them, and use them for restoration.” The work remains in the research stage, and the study did not evaluate microbial restoration treatments in agricultural fields. Still, understanding how these organisms respond to rainfall could help researchers better predict how dryland ecosystems will function as precipitation patterns change. For regions facing longer droughts or increasingly unpredictable rainfall, the findings offer another piece of the puzzle in understanding how soil ecosystems survive under difficult conditions. analysis.time: The event occurred in March 2025, with the publication date of the news report being November 12, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak was reported in Illinois, specifically involving a backyard flock of birds, a cat, and wild rats on the farm.
analysis.event: An outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) was confirmed to have infected a cat and wild rats after it nearly destroyed an Illinois farmer’s backyard flock. The analysis was conducted by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory and the University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Laboratory.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak resulted in the loss of 100 out of 105 backyard birds. Tissue testing found all 12 cat samples and 11 of 15 rat samples infected, with viral RNA also detected in the rat’s urine. The virus showed a mutation that enhances its ability to infect mammals, indicating potential for spillover.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The investigation is ongoing, and the findings were published in the CDC journal Emerging Infectious Diseases. The study highlights the need for biosecurity measures, such as keeping poultry away from wild waterfowl, controlling rodents, and preventing farm cats from scavenging dead birds.

analysis.brief_en: In March 2025, an outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) nearly destroyed an Illinois farmer’s backyard flock of 105 birds, with 100 lost. The farmer submitted samples of five birds and a rat to the University of Missouri for testing. Subsequent analysis by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory and the University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Laboratory confirmed that the cat and a second rat were infected with the same H5N1 subtype as the chicken. Tissue testing revealed all 12 cat samples and 11 of 15 rat samples were infected, with viral RNA also found in the rat’s urine. The virus carried a mutation that enhances its ability to infect mammals, suggesting potential for spillover. The findings were published in the CDC journal Emerging Infectious Diseases, highlighting the risk of rodents acting as a bridge for the virus to move between wild birds, poultry, and other mammals. The outbreak underscores the importance of biosecurity measures, such as keeping poultry away from wild waterfowl, controlling rodents, and preventing farm cats from scavenging dead birds. The investigation remains ongoing, and the report serves as a warning for farmers to remain vigilant about potential virus transmission risks.

news.content_zh: 2025 年 3 月,高致病性禽流感 (H5N1) 的 暴发 几乎消灭了伊利诺伊州农民后院的 105 只鸟,其中 100 只消失。该农民向密苏里大学提交了五只鸟和一只老鼠的样本进行测试。伊利诺伊大学厄巴纳-香槟分校兽医诊断实验室和密苏里大学兽医医学诊断实验室随后的分析证实,这只猫和另一只老鼠感染了与鸡相同的H5N1亚型。组织检测显示,所有 12 份猫样本和 15 份大鼠样本中的 11 份均被感染,在老鼠的尿液中也发现了病毒 RNA。该病毒携带 突变,增强其感染哺乳动物的能力,表明 跨物种溢出 的潜力。研究结果发表在疾病预防控制中心的期刊《新发传染病》上,强调了啮齿类动物作为病毒在 野生鸟类、家禽和其他哺乳动物之间传播的桥梁的风险。暴发 强调了生物安全措施的重要性,例如让家禽远离野生水禽、控制啮齿动物以及防止农场猫吃死鸟。调查仍在进行中,该报告警告农民对潜在的病毒 传播 风险保持警惕。

(KTVZ) -- Reports of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) are increasing among ducks and geese migrating through Oregon, with the majority of sick and dead birds being reported in the Willamette Valley. The Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife (ODFW) says the Cackling goose, a smaller subspecies of the Canada goose, appears to be the most heavily affected. ODFW is urging the public to avoid contact with sick birds and keep pets away from them. People are also advised not to capture or transport sick birds to wildlife rehabilitation centers, as there is no effective treatment for infected wild or domestic birds. The virus can spread rapidly among bird populations and potentially to other wildlife. Signs of avian influenza in birds Symptoms in wild waterfowl can include: Lethargy or inability to fly Erratic behavior or loss of coordination Cloudy eyes Swimming in circles Head shaking Some ducks may carry and spread the virus without showing symptoms. Birds that develop clinical signs typically die within 72 hours. Infected wild mammals may also appear sick, show neurological abnormalities or be found dead after consuming infected birds. How to report sick or dead birds ODFW says its Wildlife Health staff have been collecting and testing birds to monitor the outbreak. The agency does not need additional bird collections for testing at this time. However, the public is encouraged to report groups of dead birds that show no obvious signs of illness before death. Reports can be made by calling 866-968-2600 or emailing wildlife.health@odfw.oregon.gov. Due to the high volume of reports, staff may not be able to return calls. If disposing of a dead bird, ODFW recommends wearing disposable gloves and a mask and double-bagging the carcass before placing it in the trash. The public should also report sick or dead domestic birds, including chickens, turkeys and guinea fowl, to the Oregon Department of Agriculture at 503-986-4711 or 800-347-7028. Risk to people remains low According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the risk of avian influenza to people remains low. Since 2024, there have been 74 confirmed human cases of avian influenza in the United States, including three deaths. (KTVZ) -- Reports of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) are increasing among ducks and geese migrating through Oregon, with the majority of sick and dead birds being reported in the Willamette Valley. The Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife (ODFW) says the Cackling goose, a smaller subspecies of the Canada goose, appears to be the most heavily affected. ODFW is urging the public to avoid contact with sick birds and keep pets away from them. People are also advised not to capture or transport sick birds to wildlife rehabilitation centers, as there is no effective treatment for infected wild or domestic birds. The virus can spread rapidly among bird populations and potentially to other wildlife. Signs of avian influenza in birds Symptoms in wild waterfowl can include: Lethargy or inability to fly Erratic behavior or loss of coordination Cloudy eyes Swimming in circles Head shaking Some ducks may carry and spread the virus without showing symptoms. Birds that develop clinical signs typically die within 72 hours. Infected wild mammals may also appear sick, show neurological abnormalities or be found dead after consuming infected birds. How to report sick or dead birds ODFW says its Wildlife Health staff have been collecting and testing birds to monitor the outbreak. The agency does not need additional bird collections for testing at this time. However, the public is encouraged to report groups of dead birds that show no obvious signs of illness before death. Reports can be made by calling 866-968-2600 or emailing wildlife.health@odfw.oregon.gov. Due to the high volume of reports, staff may not be able to return calls. If disposing of a dead bird, ODFW recommends wearing disposable gloves and a mask and double-bagging the carcass before placing it in the trash. The public should also report sick or dead domestic birds, including chickens, turkeys and guinea fowl, to the Oregon Department of Agriculture at 503-986-4711 or 800-347-7028. Risk to people remains low According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the risk of avian influenza to people remains low. Since 2024, there have been 74 confirmed human cases of avian influenza in the United States, including three deaths. Photograph: Jim Holden/Alamy View image in fullscreen Birdkeepers must follow enhanced biosecurity measures including reporting changes in egg production and reporting suspected disease immediately. Photograph: Jim Holden/Alamy Bird flu fears prompt orders for farmers to keep poultry inside in England and Scotland Increased risk of devastating strain means restrictions imposed for second year in a row on those keeping birds Poultry and captive birds across England and Scotland must be kept inside for the second year in a row due to an increased risk of a devastating strain of bird flu. The British government has issued an England-wide avian influenza prevention zone, meaning individuals with 50 or more poultry or captive birds must house them inside. A similar designation was made across the whole of Scotland on Tuesday. Birdkeepers must also follow enhanced biosecurity measures including reporting changes in egg production and reporting suspected disease immediately to the Animal and Plant Health Agency. The government said the declaration followed an increased risk and escalating number of confirmations of the highly pathogenic avian influenza, or bird flu, in kept and wild birds. A prevention zone was also declared across all of England, Scotland and Wales in 2025. The disease has been spreading rapidly since 2014 and has devastated UK wild bird populations since the summer of 2021. It has also spread across an unusually broad range of species around the world, including in four of the five main southern elephant seal populations. In some south Atlantic colonies, more than 90% of newborn pups have died, alongside about half of all adult females. Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow? Read more The disease has also been detected in humans, with 11 deaths recorded globally between 1 January and 4 August 2025. This strain of bird flu causes illness and high death rates in birds, and flu-like symptoms and conjunctivitis in humans who come into close contact with infected animals. The British government said the current risk to human health from bird flu remained very low. The government says it does not anticipate an impact on the availability of Christmas turkeys or other seasonal poultry for consumers. The Food Safety Authority said properly cooked poultry and poultry products, including eggs, were safe to eat. The UK chief veterinary officer, Christine Middlemiss, said: “Having avian influenza confirmed in your flock can be devastating. I understand the impact this disease can have on the poultry sector and am extremely grateful for the continued cooperation of the industry.” Explore more on these topics Bird flu Farming Health England Scotland Animals news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Putin takes hard line in US talks as Ukraine says Starlink disrupted again Microsoft begins restoring services as global outage affects Outlook and Teams Florida St Patrick’s Day parade cancelled over Republican anti-DEI law, causing outrage Marco Rubio reportedly spent over $1.2m of taxpayer money traveling to son’s football games ‘Maga is dead, Maga is effeminate’: why has the manosphere rejected Trump? Photograph: Jim Holden/Alamy View image in fullscreen Birdkeepers must follow enhanced biosecurity measures including reporting changes in egg production and reporting suspected disease immediately. Photograph: Jim Holden/Alamy Bird flu fears prompt orders for farmers to keep poultry inside in England and Scotland Increased risk of devastating strain means restrictions imposed for second year in a row on those keeping birds Poultry and captive birds across England and Scotland must be kept inside for the second year in a row due to an increased risk of a devastating strain of bird flu. The British government has issued an England-wide avian influenza prevention zone, meaning individuals with 50 or more poultry or captive birds must house them inside. A similar designation was made across the whole of Scotland on Tuesday. Birdkeepers must also follow enhanced biosecurity measures including reporting changes in egg production and reporting suspected disease immediately to the Animal and Plant Health Agency. The government said the declaration followed an increased risk and escalating number of confirmations of the highly pathogenic avian influenza, or bird flu, in kept and wild birds. A prevention zone was also declared across all of England, Scotland and Wales in 2025. The disease has been spreading rapidly since 2014 and has devastated UK wild bird populations since the summer of 2021. It has also spread across an unusually broad range of species around the world, including in four of the five main southern elephant seal populations. In some south Atlantic colonies, more than 90% of newborn pups have died, alongside about half of all adult females. Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow? Read more The disease has also been detected in humans, with 11 deaths recorded globally between 1 January and 4 August 2025. This strain of bird flu causes illness and high death rates in birds, and flu-like symptoms and conjunctivitis in humans who come into close contact with infected animals. The British government said the current risk to human health from bird flu remained very low. The government says it does not anticipate an impact on the availability of Christmas turkeys or other seasonal poultry for consumers. The Food Safety Authority said properly cooked poultry and poultry products, including eggs, were safe to eat. The UK chief veterinary officer, Christine Middlemiss, said: “Having avian influenza confirmed in your flock can be devastating. I understand the impact this disease can have on the poultry sector and am extremely grateful for the continued cooperation of the industry.” Explore more on these topics Bird flu Farming Health England Scotland Animals news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Putin takes hard line in US talks as Ukraine says Starlink disrupted again Microsoft begins restoring services as global outage affects Outlook and Teams Florida St Patrick’s Day parade cancelled over Republican anti-DEI law, causing outrage Marco Rubio reportedly spent over $1.2m of taxpayer money traveling to son’s football games ‘Maga is dead, Maga is effeminate’: why has the manosphere rejected Trump? Corporate M&A Companies Coops Appointments and Resignations Interview Events MENA Dairy Congress Upcoming events Presentations Photoreports Advertising H5N1 affects 40 dairy herds in Washington in one month United States 09.11.2026 Subscribe to weekly digest Source: en.edairynews.com 593 The detection of avian influenza on dairy farms in central Washington coincides with renewed warnings about raw milk consumption. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has renewed its call for a ban on its sale following the death of a farmworker in Yakima County. The worker died on November 1, 2026, in the third fatal H5N1 case recorded in the United States, according to information compiled by Animals 24-7 and regional agricultural publications. The veterinary monitoring cited puts the number of cattle herds diagnosed over the past month in central Washington state at 40, amid new autumn outbreaks among birds and mammals. The warning from the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), addressed to state and federal lawmakers, calls for explicit bans on the retail sale and distribution of unpasteurized milk and cheeses made from it. The organization highlights the risks to children and immunocompromised people. The sale of raw fluid milk remains legal in 30 of the country's 50 states. The medical recommendations note that H5N1 replicates extensively in the mammary tissue of infected cows, resulting in high viral concentrations in raw milk. The studies cited indicate that raw milk can retain live, infectious virus for up to five weeks under conventional refrigeration. This persistence is among the reasons given for strengthening health surveillance of dairy products that have not undergone heat treatment. news.content: About us Who we are How we are run How we are funded The RSPB’s Annual Report 2025–26 Our history What's happening Nature news Our priceless protected areas The UK's Bird of the Year 2026 Big Schools’ Birdwatch RSPB Winter Raffle 2026/27 Helping nature What we do Volunteer with us Business partnerships Support us What you can do Birds and wildlife Bird A-Z Identifying birds and wildlife Feeding birds near you Declines, disease and dangers – the issues facing birds Who should I call if I am concerned about a bird? How to report crimes against wild birds Days out Visit a reserve Find an event near you Search Shop Membership Donate Search Menu Home Whats happening Back to News Bird flu impacts global review News Seabirds amongst hardest hit by avian influenza outbreaks New research has identified which groups experienced the biggest losses from bird flu outbreaks between 2000 and 2020. 11th Nov 20265 min read Mute Swan Outbreaks of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) can cause large population losses across a wide range of bird species. By combining data from 40 different mass mortality events across the world, new research shows that some bird groups, such as gulls, terns and other seabirds, appear more likely to suffer significant population losses, than others, such as waterfowl. The long-term impact of HPAI HPAI is a contagious, and potentially deadly, viral infection which spreads between birds through saliva, nasal secretions, droppings, predation and scavenging. Where outbreaks occur, thousands of birds can die, causing an initial drop in population size. Researchers at the RSPB collated datasets from across the world where bird populations were monitored before, during and after HPAI outbreaks which occurred pre-2020. They found that most populations experienced a decline immediately following outbreaks, with an average 17% drop in number of birds. In most cases, populations recovered following this initial impact and bounced back within a few years. However, in 25% of cases, populations did not recover from these initial declines within the post-outbreak monitoring period (which varied between 4-17 years). Vulnerable seabirds among most impacted Gulls, terns, penguins and ducks, experienced some of the strongest initial declines after disease outbreaks. Populations of African Penguin, Cape Cormorant, Common Pochard, Great Black-backed Gull, Peregrine Falcon, and Tufted Duck failed to recover following HPAI outbreaks. Seabirds often nest in dense colonies, living closely alongside each other, making it easy for infections to spread quickly between individuals. Their long-distance feeding routes mean it is also possible for infections to spread between distant colonies. The long-lived nature of many seabirds also means the initial impacts of mass mortality events may not become apparent until there is a shortfall in breeding age adults. However, there was also evidence of resilience in some affected populations. Waterfowl species (ducks, geese and swans) appeared to suffer less short-term population impacts. These species tend to raise large numbers of young and therefore may be able to bounce back quicker following a mortality incident. There is also evidence of natural immunity spreading rapidly amongst some affected waterfowl populations. However post-2020 we have seen an increase in the size and severity of outbreaks in these species. Common Pochard The future of HPAI Since 2020, we have seen an escalation in the impacts from the virus globally with even more species and countries affected by HPAI, and the virus now even detected on Gough Island, one of the most remote inhabited islands in the world. There has also been an increase in the severity of outbreaks occurring during the breeding season. This means as monitoring continues, we may see different and potentially more severe population impacts from post-2020 outbreaks. Since the current strain reached the UK in 2021, the greatest impacts in UK birds have been seen in seabirds, but we’re increasingly concerned about the ongoing impact on birds of prey. There is evidence of reduced breeding success in both White-tailed Eagles and Golden Eagles, with local population declines observed in Peregrine and Buzzard. The consistently high numbers of HPAI cases being seen in Mute Swans over a number of years is also worrying. Continued population monitoring is essential for making sure we are able to identify species most vulnerable to the impacts of HPAI. Action to reduce additional stressors on vulnerable wild bird populations and identifying ways we can support the recovery of threatened populations will be key to protecting our most vulnerable species through future HPAI outbreaks. This work was funded by our RSPB Avian Flu Appeal, which directly supports research and action addressing the threat of HPAI to our wild birds. Thank you so much to everyone who supported this appeal. You can now help our scientists undertake vital research so we can save our wildlife by donating to our Wildlife Disease Fund. How to report crimes against wild birds Days out Visit a reserve Find an event near you Search Shop Membership Donate Search Menu Home Whats happening Back to News Bird flu impacts global review News Seabirds amongst hardest hit by avian influenza outbreaks New research has identified which groups experienced the biggest losses from bird flu outbreaks between 2000 and 2020. 11th Nov 20265 min read Mute Swan Outbreaks of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) can cause large population losses across a wide range of bird species. By combining data from 40 different mass mortality events across the world, new research shows that some bird groups, such as gulls, terns and other seabirds, appear more likely to suffer significant population losses, than others, such as waterfowl. The long-term impact of HPAI HPAI is a contagious, and potentially deadly, viral infection which spreads between birds through saliva, nasal secretions, droppings, predation and scavenging. Where outbreaks occur, thousands of birds can die, causing an initial drop in population size. Researchers at the RSPB collated datasets from across the world where bird populations were monitored before, during and after HPAI outbreaks which occurred pre-2020. They found that most populations experienced a decline immediately following outbreaks, with an average 17% drop in number of birds. In most cases, populations recovered following this initial impact and bounced back within a few years. However, in 25% of cases, populations did not recover from these initial declines within the post-outbreak monitoring period (which varied between 4-17 years). Vulnerable seabirds among most impacted Gulls, terns, penguins and ducks, experienced some of the strongest initial declines after disease outbreaks. Populations of African Penguin, Cape Cormorant, Common Pochard, Great Black-backed Gull, Peregrine Falcon, and Tufted Duck failed to recover following HPAI outbreaks. Seabirds often nest in dense colonies, living closely alongside each other, making it easy for infections to spread quickly between individuals. Their long-distance feeding routes mean it is also possible for infections to spread between distant colonies. The long-lived nature of many seabirds also means the initial impacts of mass mortality events may not become apparent until there is a shortfall in breeding age adults. However, there was also evidence of resilience in some affected populations. Waterfowl species (ducks, geese and swans) appeared to suffer less short-term population impacts. These species tend to raise large numbers of young and therefore may be able to bounce back quicker following a mortality incident. There is also evidence of natural immunity spreading rapidly amongst some affected waterfowl populations. However post-2020 we have seen an increase in the size and severity of outbreaks in these species. Common Pochard The future of HPAI Since 2020, we have seen an escalation in the impacts from the virus globally with even more species and countries affected by HPAI, and the virus now even detected on Gough Island, one of the most remote inhabited islands in the world. There has also been an increase in the severity of outbreaks occurring during the breeding season. This means as monitoring continues, we may see different and potentially more severe population impacts from post-2020 outbreaks. Since the current strain reached the UK in 2021, the greatest impacts in UK birds have been seen in seabirds, but we’re increasingly concerned about the ongoing impact on birds of prey. There is evidence of reduced breeding success in both White-tailed Eagles and Golden Eagles, with local population declines observed in Peregrine and Buzzard. The consistently high numbers of HPAI cases being seen in Mute Swans over a number of years is also worrying. Continued population monitoring is essential for making sure we are able to identify species most vulnerable to the impacts of HPAI. Action to reduce additional stressors on vulnerable wild bird populations and identifying ways we can support the recovery of threatened populations will be key to protecting our most vulnerable species through future HPAI outbreaks. This work was funded by our RSPB Avian Flu Appeal, which directly supports research and action addressing the threat of HPAI to our wild birds. Thank you so much to everyone who supported this appeal. You can now help our scientists undertake vital research so we can save our wildlife by donating to our Wildlife Disease Fund. analysis.time: The study analyzed outbreaks between 2000 and 2020, with the latest update on the impact of HPAI in the UK in 2021. The current report was published on 2026-11-11.
analysis.location_and_population: The report covers global bird populations, with specific mention of UK seabirds and birds of prey, including Mute Swans, White-tailed Eagles, Golden Eagles, Peregrine Falcons, and Buzzards.
analysis.event: New research conducted by the RSPB identified that seabirds, such as gulls, terns, penguins, and ducks, experienced significant population losses during HPAI outbreaks between 2000 and 2020. Some populations, like African Penguins, Cape Cormorants, Common Pochards, Great Black-backed Gulls, and Tufted Ducks, did not recover within the post-outbreak monitoring period.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study found that most bird populations experienced a decline of up to 17% immediately after HPAI outbreaks, with some species failing to recover. The long-distance feeding routes of seabirds and their nesting habits in dense colonies increase the risk of rapid infection spread. The report also notes an increase in outbreak severity since 2020, particularly during the breeding season.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The RSPB is emphasizing the need for continued population monitoring to identify species most vulnerable to HPAI. Action to reduce additional stressors on vulnerable bird populations and support recovery efforts is being prioritized. The report is based on data from 40 mass mortality events and is ongoing, with potential for more severe impacts in the future.

analysis.brief_en: A new study by the RSPB highlights that seabirds, including gulls, terns, penguins, and ducks, have been among the hardest hit by avian influenza outbreaks between 2000 and 2020. Researchers analyzed data from 40 global mass mortality events and found that most bird populations experienced a decline of up to 17% immediately after outbreaks, with some species failing to recover within the post-outbreak monitoring period. The report notes that seabirds often nest in dense colonies, facilitating rapid infection spread, and their long-distance feeding routes may contribute to the virus spreading between distant colonies. Since 2020, there has been an increase in outbreak severity, particularly during the breeding season, with concerns about the ongoing impact on birds of prey and Mute Swans. The RSPB is calling for continued monitoring and action to support vulnerable populations and mitigate future risks from HPAI.

news.source_body_en: A new study by the RSPB highlights that seabirds, including gulls, terns, penguins, and ducks, have been among the hardest hit by avian influenza outbreaks between 2000 and 2020. Researchers analyzed data from 40 global mass mortality events and found that most bird populations experienced a decline of up to 17% immediately after outbreaks, with some species failing to recover within the post-outbreak monitoring period. The report notes that seabirds often nest in dense colonies, facilitating rapid infection spread, and their long-distance feeding routes may contribute to the virus spreading between distant colonies. Since 2020, there has been an increase in outbreak severity, particularly during the breeding season, with concerns about the ongoing impact on birds of prey and Mute Swans. The RSPB is calling for continued monitoring and action to support vulnerable populations and mitigate future risks from HPAI.
news.content_zh: 一项由RSPB进行的新研究指出,包括海鸥、 terns、企鹅和鸭子在内的海鸟在2000年至2020年间受到了暴发的严重影响。研究人员分析了全球40起大规模死亡率事件的数据,发现大多数鸟类种群在暴发后立即下降了高达17%,一些物种在暴发后的监测期间未能恢复。报告指出,海鸟通常在密集的群体中筑巢,这有助于病毒的快速传播,而它们的长途觅食路线可能促进了病毒在不同群体之间的扩散。自2020年以来,暴发的严重程度有所增加,尤其是在繁殖季节,人们对这种疾病对猛禽和哑天鹅的持续影响表示担忧。RSPB呼吁继续监测并采取行动,以支持易受影响的种群并减轻未来高致病性禽流感(HPAI)带来的风险。

news.content: English Spanish Our Categories Entrepreneurs Tech Talent Energy Oil & Gas Mining Health Automotive Aerospace Finance & Fintech Infrastructure Sustainability Professional Services E-Commerce & Retail Agribusiness & Food Logistics Mobility Trade & Investment Policy & Economy Cybersecurity AI, Cloud & Data Chemicals Multimedia Podcast Videos Audio Articles Opinion Expert Contributor Startup Contributor Goverment Embassy Chamber of Commerce Industry Association Type Spotlight Join our expert contributor program All Multimedia Expert Contributor Entrepreneurs Tech Talent Energy Oil & Gas Mining Health Automotive Aerospace Finance & Fintech Infrastructure Sustainability Professional Services E-Commerce & Retail Agribusiness & Food Logistics Mobility Trade & Investment Policy & Economy Cybersecurity AI, Cloud & Data Chemicals < > Home > Agribusiness & Food > Article H5N1 Outbreak in Yucatan Puts Poultry Sector on High Alert Share it! WhatsAppLinkedInTwitterFacebookEmailShare By MBN Staff MBN staff Tue, 11/10/2026 12:04 3 min read DIA READ ARTICLE Ready to read 0:00 1x Following the confirmation of an H5N1 avian influenza outbreak in Yucatan, Mexico’s animal protein sector faces an urgent biosecurity test. Federal authorities and commercial operators are rapidly executing containment protocols, reevaluating risk frameworks, and addressing potential supply chain disruptions across domestic agricultural markets. ___ Mexico’s animal protein sector is confronting a biosecurity test following the official confirmation of a highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza outbreak on a commercial laying-hen farm located in the Yucatan Peninsula. This animal health event was formally reported by the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) based on comprehensive epidemiological data submitted directly by Mexican agricultural authorities. According to these official filings, the virus was positively identified within a large-scale, intensive commercial flock comprising 225,860 laying hens situated specifically in the municipality of Uman. Prior to veterinary intervention and the implementation of emergency sanitary measures, the affected flock recorded 862 natural mortalities. In response to the viral detection, federal and regional sanitary authorities, —notably SENASICA and its specialized Central Commission for Animal Health (CPA) branch, swiftly executed mandatory containment protocols. These emergency measures included the immediate establishment of a strict 10km risk perimeter surrounding the index premises alongside the total depopulation of the remaining 224,998 birds to prevent any further lateral transmission. The unfolding details of this sanitary operation were extensively documented via The Poultry Site report. Marking Mexico’s first confirmed commercial poultry outbreak since May 2024, the incident has immediately reverberated across domestic protein supply chains, prompting agricultural conglomerates, major poultry integrators, and B2B supply chain directors to urgently reevaluate their internal biosecurity frameworks, risk management strategies, and contingency distribution plans. The reemergence of the H5N1 virus underscores the persistent and structural vulnerabilities confronting intensive industrial poultry production corridors across the country. While Mexican sanitary authorities and leading protein producers have consistently maintained heightened surveillance networks following past global epizootic waves, localized viral incursions continue to pose severe and unpredictable threats to regional production capacity, table egg output volumes, and wholesale price stability. As previously explored in analytical assessments regarding Mexico's Agrifood Sector Navigates Market Changes, ongoing structural adjustments, mounting climate pressures, and evolving regulatory mandates are continuously reshaping domestic agricultural corridors. For major national market participants such as Industrias Bachoco and Pilgrim’s Pride México, the timing of the Yucatan outbreak compounds an already complex and multifaceted array of macroeconomic headwinds. The broader Mexican agrifood landscape in late 2026 exhibits a striking structural dichotomy, defined by robust foreign direct investment inflows running parallel to severe primary production challenges, as detailed further in Mexico's Food Industry Faces Staple Shortages and Trade Shifts. Animal protein producers are already actively navigating fluctuating feed grain acquisition costs, stringent environmental compliance standards, and shifting consumer purchasing habits set against the backdrop of broader inflationary pressures. The introduction of an acute avian influenza event adds substantial logistical friction, threatening regional table egg distribution networks and intensifying cost-push inflation across both retail channels and commercial food service operations. WhatsAppLinkedInTwitterFacebookEmailShare By MBN Staff MBN staff Tue, 11/10/2026 12:04 3 min read DIA READ ARTICLE Ready to read 0:00 1x Following the confirmation of an H5N1 avian influenza outbreak in Yucatan, Mexico’s animal protein sector faces an urgent biosecurity test. Federal authorities and commercial operators are rapidly executing containment protocols, reevaluating risk frameworks, and addressing potential supply chain disruptions across domestic agricultural markets. ___ Mexico’s animal protein sector is confronting a biosecurity test following the official confirmation of a highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza outbreak on a commercial laying-hen farm located in the Yucatan Peninsula. This animal health event was formally reported by the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) based on comprehensive epidemiological data submitted directly by Mexican agricultural authorities. According to these official filings, the virus was positively identified within a large-scale, intensive commercial flock comprising 225,860 laying hens situated specifically in the municipality of Uman. Prior to veterinary intervention and the implementation of emergency sanitary measures, the affected flock recorded 862 natural mortalities. In response to the viral detection, federal and regional sanitary authorities, —notably SENASICA and its specialized Central Commission for Animal Health (CPA) branch, swiftly executed mandatory containment protocols. These emergency measures included the immediate establishment of a strict 10km risk perimeter surrounding the index premises alongside the total depopulation of the remaining 224,998 birds to prevent any further lateral transmission. The unfolding details of this sanitary operation were extensively documented via The Poultry Site report. Marking Mexico’s first confirmed commercial poultry outbreak since May 2024, the incident has immediately reverberated across domestic protein supply chains, prompting agricultural conglomerates, major poultry integrators, and B2B supply chain directors to urgently reevaluate their internal biosecurity frameworks, risk management strategies, and contingency distribution plans. The reemergence of the H5N1 virus underscores the persistent and structural vulnerabilities confronting intensive industrial poultry production corridors across the country. While Mexican sanitary authorities and leading protein producers have consistently maintained heightened surveillance networks following past global epizootic waves, localized viral incursions continue to pose severe and unpredictable threats to regional production capacity, table egg output volumes, and wholesale price stability. As previously explored in analytical assessments regarding Mexico's Agrifood Sector Navigates Market Changes, ongoing structural adjustments, mounting climate pressures, and evolving regulatory mandates are continuously reshaping domestic agricultural corridors. For major national market participants such as Industrias Bachoco and Pilgrim’s Pride México, the timing of the Yucatan outbreak compounds an already complex and multifaceted array of macroeconomic headwinds. The broader Mexican agrifood landscape in late 2026 exhibits a striking structural dichotomy, defined by robust foreign direct investment inflows running parallel to severe primary production challenges, as detailed further in Mexico's Food Industry Faces Staple Shortages and Trade Shifts. Animal protein producers are already actively navigating fluctuating feed grain acquisition costs, stringent environmental compliance standards, and shifting consumer purchasing habits set against the backdrop of broader inflationary pressures. The introduction of an acute avian influenza event adds substantial logistical friction, threatening regional table egg distribution networks and intensifying cost-push inflation across both retail channels and commercial food service operations. news.content_zh: 2026 年 11 月 10 日,墨西哥尤卡坦半岛乌曼的一个商业蛋鸡养殖场确认了 H5N1 禽流感 暴发。世界动物卫生组织 (WOAH) 根据墨西哥农业当局的数据报告了这一事件。在实施遏制措施之前,暴发 导致 862 人自然死亡。包括 SENASICA 及其中央动物健康委员会 (CPA) 在内的联邦和地区卫生当局迅速执行了相关协议,例如建立 10 公里的风险范围并减少剩余 224,998 只鸟类的数量,以防止进一步的 传播。该事件引发了对整个家禽行业生物安全框架和风险管理策略的紧急重新评估,凸显了该行业的脆弱性。暴发 还给零售和商业食品服务运营带来了物流挑战并加剧了成本推动型通货膨胀。这一事件凸显了墨西哥家禽生产和供应链持续面临的风险。

analysis.brief_en: Oregon wildlife officials have reported an increase in the number of waterfowl infected with bird flu across the Willamette Valley, according to a news report from NPR for Oregonians. The report, published on November 13, 2026, highlights the growing concern but does not provide specific case counts, death tolls, or exposure numbers. It also does not detail the exact response measures or investigation status. The situation is being tracked by local authorities, but further information is needed to assess the full scale and risk of the outbreak. This report serves as an alert about the potential spread of bird flu among wildlife, which could have implications for public health and animal welfare.

news.title_zh: 俄勒冈州野生动物官员报告威拉米特山谷感染禽流感的水禽数量不断增加 - NPR for Oregonians
news.source_body_en: Oregon wildlife officials have reported an increase in the number of waterfowl infected with bird flu across the Willamette Valley, according to a news report from NPR for Oregonians. The report, published on November 13, 2026, highlights the growing concern but does not provide specific case counts, death tolls, or exposure numbers. It also does not detail the exact response measures or investigation status. The situation is being tracked by local authorities, but further information is needed to assess the full scale and risk of the outbreak. This report serves as an alert about the potential spread of bird flu among wildlife, which could have implications for public health and animal welfare.
news.content_zh: 据美国国家公共广播电台俄勒冈州新闻报道,俄勒冈州野生动物官员报告称,威拉米特山谷感染禽流感的水禽数量有所增加。该报告于 2026 年 11 月 13 日发布,强调了人们日益增长的担忧,但没有提供具体的病例数、死亡人数或暴露人数。它还没有详细说明确切的应对措施或调查状态。地方当局正在跟踪情况,但需要进一步的信息来评估 暴发 的全面规模和风险。这份报告对禽流感在野生动物中潜在传播的可能性发出了警报,这可能对公共健康和动物福利产生影响。

(Savo Ilic - stock.adobe.com) By Ania Keenan, KIRO 7 News November 12, 2026 at 8:07 am PST YAKIMA COUNTY, Wash. — In a list of social media posts on Wednesday evening, United Farm Workers Union said that at least one person had died after being exposed to Avian Flu while working on a dairy farm in Yakima County. According to Yakima County, three people have been infected, but the risk to the general public remains low. The union said many more workers are infected and dealing with symptoms ranging from mild to severe. The organization that represents thousands of farm workers across the country said the infections came from caring for dairy herds infected with the illness. Data from the county shows that since the beginning of October, 33 cases of avian flu have been discovered in cattle. The union reported that workers said they were given gloves, masks, and other protective gear, but they are not being given information on vaccinations or flu testing. ©2026 Cox Media Group 0 View Comments Most Read

Yakima County confirmed three individuals have been infected, though the risk to the general public is considered low. The union also noted that many more workers are infected and experiencing symptoms ranging from mild to severe. Despite being provided with protective gear, workers are not receiving information on vaccinations or flu testing. The situation is under investigation, with no further details on the spread or containment measures provided in the evidence.

news.content: U.S. News Politics AI Politics Tech Fact Check Sports Global Iran War Russia-Ukraine Middle East China And Asia Live Blog Better Planet All World News Lifestyle Family & Parenting Entertainment Travel Pets Automotive Relationships Science Health Personal Finance Better Workplaces Readers Choice Opinion My Turn All Opinion Rankings Health Finance Products Education Workplaces Corporate Responsibility All Rankings Watch The 1600 The Royal Report Unconventional From The Paddock Newsmakers Extra Newsletters Dare to Dream Events Essays Podcasts Vantage Insights Magazine CEO Circle Announcements Leadership Dev Pragad Subscribe Sign In U.S. NewsPoliticsAI PoliticsTechFact CheckSports Global Iran WarRussia-UkraineMiddle EastChina And AsiaLive BlogBetter PlanetAll World News Lifestyle Family & ParentingEntertainmentTravelPetsAutomotiveRelationshipsScienceHealthPersonal FinanceBetter WorkplacesReaders Choice Opinion My TurnAll Opinion Rankings HealthCorporate ResponsibilityFinanceProductsEducationWorkAll Rankings Watch The 1600The Royal ReportUnconventionalFrom The PaddockNewsmakers Social FacebookInstagramYouTubeRedditTikTokTwitter/X Extra NewslettersDare to DreamEventsEssaysPodcastsVantageInsightsMagazineCEO CircleAnnouncementsLeadershipDev Pragad The number of people infected by an outbreak of avian flu in Washington State is much higher than initially reported, a farm workers' union has revealed. An outbreak of the H5 influenza virus has spread rapidly throughout the Yakima Valley, infecting over 30 dairy herds and causing the death of at least one person. County officials claim three people have been infected with the virus following exposure at a dairy, but United Farm Workers (UFW) says the real numbers have been vastly underreported. “We have now connected with a number of workers and have confirmed that more workers are sick with avian flu symptoms who have not been tested,” the UFW said in a statement on X. “Their symptoms range from very mild to very severe. “The workers report symptoms that range from mild upper respiratory infection with pinkeye to severe flu symptoms with bone pain, severe cough and high fever. We do not have reports that indicate human to human transmission, just workplace exposure to infected animals and milk.” Newsweek has contacted the UFW and county health officials for additional comment. The UFW cites an ongoing ICE surge in Yakima Valley as part of the reason for the depressed figures, claiming their presence has made many workers reluctant to engage with public agencies and fearful of disobeying their employers. The lack of proper sick pay and PPE training has also helped spread the virus and encouraged workers with milder symptoms not to report the infection. “UFW staff are trying to support sick workers, but there are many barriers,” the union added. “Workers with milder symptoms are reluctant to be tested or miss work because sick cattle still need care. Workers are very afraid of ICE-related retaliation if they don’t follow employers instructions.” The Yakima County health board reported the death of a resident on Sunday after they contracted avian flu through exposure to infected cattle. The individual, who had underlying health conditions, was hospitalized after experiencing severe illness and died shortly afterwards. Their identity has not been revealed. “The Yakima health district offers its heartfelt condolences to the individual’s family, friends, and loved ones during this difficult time,” the health board said in a statement. Two other deaths have been linked to avian flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The CDC has reported more than 70 human infections throughout the U.S. since the start of the outbreak, although there have been no recorded instances of person-to-person transmission and the risk to the general populace remains low. Farm workers remain one of the groups with the highest risk of contracting the virus due to their exposure to infected cattle. “Protecting dairy workers protects everyone,” the UFW said. “As a reminder, consumers are not at any reasonable risk from consuming pasteurized milk. The front line of this risk, the human firewall, are the workers in the dairies (and the workers in the plants who process the raw fluid milk).” Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Ben Kelly and Cristina Diciu. The CDC has reported more than 70 human infections throughout the U.S. since the start of the outbreak, although there have been no recorded instances of person-to-person transmission and the risk to the general populace remains low. Farm workers remain one of the groups with the highest risk of contracting the virus due to their exposure to infected cattle. “Protecting dairy workers protects everyone,” the UFW said. “As a reminder, consumers are not at any reasonable risk from consuming pasteurized milk. The front line of this risk, the human firewall, are the workers in the dairies (and the workers in the plants who process the raw fluid milk).” Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Ben Kelly and Cristina Diciu. This development underscores the ongoing challenge of managing avian influenza outbreaks in livestock, which may pose risks to both animal and human health.

news.source_body_en: The article titled 'Bird Flu's Wildlife Toll Raises New Conservation Questions' by Nature World News, published on 2026-11-12, discusses the impact of H5N1 bird flu on wildlife, particularly in Papua New Guinea, where it has raised concerns about conservation and extinction risks. While the piece highlights the broader implications of H5N1 on ecosystems, it does not provide specific case or death counts. Instead, it focuses on the broader context of wildlife health and environmental changes, such as the effects of climate change on marine life and the role of fungi in restoring degraded grasslands. The article also touches on other related topics, including the behavior of clownfish during marine heatwaves and the potential of AI in biodiversity research. However, it does not detail any specific response measures or investigation status related to H5N1. The piece serves as a general overview rather than a report on confirmed outbreaks or targeted interventions.
news.content_zh: 《自然世界新闻》于 2026 年 11 月 12 日发表的题为《禽流感对野生动物造成的死亡引发了新的保护问题》的文章讨论了 H5N1 禽流感对野生动物的影响,特别是在巴布亚新几内亚,引发了人们对保护和灭绝风险的担忧。虽然这篇文章强调了 H5N1 对生态系统的更广泛影响,但它没有提供具体病例或死亡人数。相反,它侧重于野生动物健康和环境变化的更广泛背景,例如气候变化对海洋生物的影响以及真菌在恢复退化草原中的作用。文章还涉及其他相关主题,包括海洋热浪期间小丑鱼的行为以及人工智能在生物多样性研究中的潜力。不过,它没有详细说明与H5N1相关的任何具体应对措施或调查情况。该文章作为总体概述,而不是关于已确认的 暴发 或有针对性的干预措施的报告。

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 13, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Avian Influenza Hemagglutinin Mutation Hotspots Drive Cross-Species Spread and Thermal Resilience by November 12, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Avian Influenza Hemagglutinin Mutation Hotspots Drive Cross-Species Spread and Thermal Resilience Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A comprehensive study mapping the adaptive landscape of avian influenza A(H9N2) hemagglutinin has revealed how specific amino acid substitution hotspots govern viral cross-species potential, antibody evasion, and environmental thermostability. Avian influenza A(H9N2) has circulated globally across avian hosts for nearly six decades following its initial detection in Wisconsin in 1966. Over subsequent decades, the virus has established widespread endemicity in poultry populations across multiple geographic regions, creating persistent agricultural burdens and public health concerns. Beyond domestic avian infections, H9N2 serves as an established reservoir capable of infecting diverse animal hosts and donating internal gene segments to emerging zoonotic influenza strains, including H5N1 and H7N9. In many poultry-dense settings, H9N2 has become the predominant subtype, complicating disease control because conventional inactivated vaccines frequently fail to provide durable protection against divergent field strains. To address these evolutionary challenges, investigators systematically mapped the genetic determinants within the viral surface glycoprotein that enable H9N2 to alter antigenicity, adapt to mammalian cells, and endure thermal stress. The viral hemagglutinin surface glycoprotein mediates host cell entry and represents the primary target of neutralizing antibodies, placing it at the center of antigenic drift and vaccine formulation. Over prolonged circulation, H9N2 hemagglutinin has diversified into major phylogenetic lineages, including Y439, G1, and BJ94, with BJ94 further dividing into more than sixteen antigenically distinct subgroups exhibiting limited cross-reactivity. To resolve the specific mutational patterns driving this diversity, investigators examined 13,984 full-length hemagglutinin coding sequences retrieved from public databases through June 2025. This curated sequence repository encompassed isolates from four primary host groups: 13,014 sequences from domestic avians, 837 from wild birds, 110 from human clinical cases, and 23 from swine. By aligning these coding sequences with multiple sequence alignment algorithms and segregating them by host origin, the researchers established an extensive baseline to evaluate how natural selection operates across different species boundaries. To quantify amino acid variation across the surface glycoprotein, researchers calculated site-specific Shannon entropy values across all 13,984 sequences, establishing an entropy threshold of 0.2 or greater to classify 179 positions as highly variable substitution hotspots. Each identified site harbored at least two distinct amino acid variants, with residues HA66, HA145, and HA168 exhibiting the greatest diversity. Site 168 displayed the highest overall entropy score of 2.63 across fourteen distinct substitutions, followed by site 145 with an entropy value of 1.81. Cross-species correlation analyses revealed that hotspot substitution profiles in avian isolates closely mirrored those in human isolates, yielding a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.99. Conversely, wild bird isolates displayed the lowest similarity to human isolates, registering a Pearson coefficient of 0.77. At residue 145, serine predominated in wild birds while aspartic acid dominated in poultry and humans. At residue 168, serine predominated in wild birds, alanine in poultry, and human isolates harbored both alanine and asparagine variants, underscoring domestic poultry as an essential transitional reservoir. Recognizing that conventional evolutionary surveillance methods suffer from intrinsic constraints, the authors developed a high-resolution experimental strategy to interrogate hotspot variation. Standard phylogenetic monitoring remains strictly retrospective, restricted to mutations already established in circulating isolates, while traditional in vitro selections rely upon spontaneous mutagenesis that samples mutational space unevenly. To overcome these limitations, the research team constructed a focused deep mutational scanning library targeting all 179 entropy-defined hotspot sites. Using quick-change site-directed mutagenesis, investigators introduced degenerate random codons into each hotspot position within the hemagglutinin gene of the reverse-genetics plasmid rgBJ16/13, representing the A/chicken/Beijing/16/2013 strain. Plasmid pools generated from at least five hundred bacterial colonies per site were harvested and pooled. The resulting hemagglutinin plasmid library was cotransfected into HEK-293T cells alongside seven complementary genomic plasmids encoding the internal segments of rgBJ16/13 to rescue viable viral progeny, generating a primary passage-zero stock that was subsequently amplified in Madin-Darby canine kidney cells. The resulting deep mutational scanning virus library was evaluated using barcoded subamplicon sequencing with unique molecular identifiers to accurately quantify substitution frequencies. The reverse genetics procedure successfully rescued viral variants across all 179 targeted hotspot positions. While initial rescue efficiency for 91.6 percent of individual hotspot sites proved lower than that of parental wild-type rgBJ16/13, sites HA150, HA198, and HA264 showed significantly enhanced rescue, with HA198 reaching a 2.7-fold increase over wild type. Following amplification, deep sequencing revealed that 94.4 percent of hotspot positions maintained substitution frequencies below one percent, with site HA181 exhibiting the highest frequency at 5.4 percent, alongside elevated frequencies at HA115 and HA179. Comparing sitewise library frequencies to the Shannon entropy of natural strains revealed no significant correlation (Pearson R = 0.092), confirming that the experimental library captured unexplored mutational space beyond circulating strains. In contrast, initial rescue efficiency positively correlated with final amplified frequency (Pearson R = 0.22), confirming the predictive value of rescue dynamics. To identify which hotspot residues mediate escape from humoral immunity, the investigators subjected the viral library to three consecutive rounds of in vitro selection using chicken vaccine antiserum raised against rgBJ16/13 at an eighty percent neutralizing concentration. Deep sequencing performed after three rounds of immune selection revealed that selective pressure focused almost exclusively on substitutions at amino acid position 164. Parallel selection using wild-type virus carrying arginine at position 164 confirmed this focus, enriching for a glutamine substitution across two out of three independent biological replicates. To validate these findings, the authors engineered individual recombinant viruses carrying specific substitutions at position 164 and conducted plaque reduction neutralization tests. Analysis of area under the curve measurements demonstrated that viruses carrying 164Q, 164H, 164V, or 164L escaped neutralization by 164R antiserum, causing an approximately one- to two-fold reduction in neutralizing efficacy. Lineage comparisons further revealed that position 164 possesses distinctive lineage-specific profiles, with arginine dominating Y439, glutamine dominating G1, and BJ94 maintaining both variants, establishing residue 164 as an essential determinant of antigenic drift. The investigation subsequently examined host-dependent viral replication dynamics by serially passaging the mixed hotspot library through five consecutive rounds in two distinct biological environments: mammalian Madin-Darby canine kidney cells and ten-day-old embryonated chicken eggs. Over the five serial passages, viral titers displayed contrasting trajectories, increasing progressively in canine cell culture while showing a relative decrease during propagation in embryonated eggs. Next-generation sequencing performed on fifth-passage viral populations revealed profound, system-specific alterations in substitution profiles. In mammalian cell culture, an asparagine-to-histidine substitution at residue 115 (N115H) underwent rapid positive selection, expanding from baseline library levels to constitute 54.6 percent of the total viral population by the fifth passage. In marked contrast, passaging within embryonated chicken eggs selected for entirely distinct genetic alterations, leading to the enrichment of an S334G substitution to 73.5 percent abundance alongside an L224R substitution at 19.5 percent frequency, demonstrating that host cellular environments impose divergent selective pressures upon the avian influenza mutational repertoire. Statistical correlation analyses of substitution frequencies further illuminated the structural divergence between the two host-passaged viral populations. The fifth-passage population harvested from mammalian cell culture maintained a strong positive correlation with the original input library, registering a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.84, which indicated that despite the strong enrichment of N115H, broad genetic diversity across other hotspot positions was largely preserved. Conversely, passage through embryonated eggs triggered extensive restructuring of the mutational spectrum, yielding a low Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.14 when compared to the starting library. To confirm whether the dominant mammalian mutation conferred a measurable fitness advantage, researchers assessed multi-cycle replication kinetics in confluent canine kidney cells infected at a multiplicity of infection of 0.005. Growth curve analyses across three independent biological replicates demonstrated that recombinant viruses bearing the N115H substitution attained significantly higher infectious titers than parental wild-type rgBJ16/13 at 12, 24, and 36 hours post-infection, establishing that this hotspot substitution enhances viral replication efficiency in mammalian systems. In addition to host adaptation and immune evasion, the researchers evaluated hemagglutinin environmental stability, an essential physical parameter that influences viral persistence, transmission dynamics, and zoonotic potential. To identify substitutions increasing structural resilience, the 179-pool hotspot library was subjected to thermal selection at 52.5 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes, an exposure that inactivates over 90 percent of wild-type rgBJ16/13. Normalized plaque assays revealed that substitution pools at positions 14, 134, 218, 302, and 436 conferred markedly enhanced heat tolerance. Deep sequencing of eleven heat-selected sites—positions 4, 13, 14, 40, 134, 176, 218, 230, 302, 306, and 436—demonstrated a drastic reduction in sequence entropy, yielding single, heat-resistant amino acids. To validate these thermal phenotypes, authors tested purified viral variants carrying I134L and L230S within the receptor-binding domain and V306L within the stem region. Inactivation assays across a temperature gradient from 50 to 55 degrees Celsius confirmed that all three substitutions consistently increased heat resistance relative to wild-type virus. By linking computational entropy calculations derived from natural sequence databases directly to high-throughput experimental mutagenesis and phenotypic selection, this research establishes an integrated functional map of avian influenza hemagglutinin evolvability. The authors noted that whereas residue 164 exhibits extensive polymorphism among circulating H9N2 viruses, this identical position remains strictly conserved across other avian influenza subtypes such as H5 and H7, illustrating why reliance on passive sequence monitoring alone fails to anticipate emerging evolutionary trajectories. Furthermore, the exclusion of conserved epitopes from the library ensured that experimental screening focused specifically on regions possessing genuine adaptive plasticity rather than structural fragility. These findings demonstrate that H9N2 antigenic diversity, cross-species replication competence, and environmental stability are orchestrated by a discrete set of mutable hotspots that can be systematically identified and functionally characterized prior to their widespread emergence in nature. Consequently, the authors conclude that this high-throughput deep mutational scanning framework provides an essential scientific platform for predictive viral risk assessment, proactive molecular surveillance of field strains, and the rational engineering of stabilized, broadly protective next-generation poultry vaccines.
